Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned the condition of the disbelievers among the People of the Book and the polytheists, and grouped them together in the warning and made them among the People of the Fire, their obstinacy intensified, their corruption increased, and they strove to harm the Muslims in every way. Then Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿O My servants who have believed﴾. He attributed them to Himself after addressing them, as an honouring and a dignifying, and "who have believed" is a descriptive qualifier, either clarifying or distinguishing. ﴿Indeed, My earth is spacious﴾: if you are in straitness in Makkah because of the public manifestation of faith, and in the scheming of the disbelievers against you, then leave it, so that My worship alone may be made easy for you and that it may be made smooth for you.

103 Al-Zajjaj said: They were commanded to emigrate from the place in which the worship of Allah is not possible for them. Likewise, it is obligatory upon whoever is in a land where sins are committed and he is unable to change that, to emigrate to where he can prepare to worship Allah with the worship due to Him.

Mutarrif ibn al-Shikhkhir said: The meaning is: indeed My mercy is spacious and My provision for you is wide, so seek it in the earth.

It was also said: The meaning is: indeed My earth, which is the earth of Paradise, is spacious, so worship Me until I make you inherit it.

The accusative of ﴿iyaya﴾ is by a hidden verb, meaning: so worship Me.

Then He, glory be to Him, frightened them with death in order to make the matter of emigration easy for them, and said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death; then to Us you will be returned﴾. That is: every soul among souls will certainly experience the bitterness of death, so leaving homelands and parting from brothers and close friends will not be hard for you. Then to Allah is the return, by death and resurrection, not to anything else. So every living being is on a journey to the abode of permanence, however long he remains in this abode.

﴿And those who believed and did righteous deeds — We will surely settle them in lofty chambers of Paradise﴾. In this is encouragement to emigration, and that the reward of one who emigrates is to be in the chambers of Paradise. The meaning of ﹙lanubawwi'annahum﹚ is: We will surely cause them to descend into the chambers of Paradise, and they are its upper stories. So the accusative of ﹙ghurafan﹚ is either as the second object, by implication of ﹙nunzilannahum﹚ (We will cause them to descend), or as an adverb of place without implication, since ﹙nubawwi'annahum﹚ is transitive only to one object; or it is accusative by removal of the preposition, by extension, meaning: in the chambers of Paradise, and it is derived from ﹙mabaa'a﹚, which is descending.

Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, al-Jahdari, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﹙ya 'ibadi﹚ with the ya sukun, while the rest read it with fatha.

Ibn 'Amir read ﹙inna ardi﹚ with fatha on the ya, while the rest read it with sukun.

al-Sulami and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read ﹙yarji'un﹚ with the underdot (third person), while the rest read it with the top dot (second person).

Ibn Mas'ud, al-A'mash, Yahya ibn Wathhab, and Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﹙lanathwiyannahum﹚ with the thaa' (three dots) in place of the baa' (one dot), while the rest read it with the baa'. The meaning of ﹙lanathwiyannahum﹚ with the three-dot thaa' is: We will surely give them chambers in which they will dwell, from ﹙al-thawa﹚, which is residing.

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "thawa al-rajul" when he resided, and "athwaytuhu" when you cause him to descend into a dwelling in which he remains.

Al-Akhfash said: This reading does not please me, because you do not say "athwaytuhu al-dar"; rather you say "fi al-dar," and there is no prepositional particle on the second object in the verse. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: It is by intending the prepositional particle, then it was deleted, as you say "amartuka al-khayr," meaning "bi al-khayr."

Then He, glory be to Him, described those chambers, saying: ﴿Flowing beneath them are rivers﴾, that is: beneath the chambers; ﴿abiding therein﴾, that is: in the chambers, never dying forever; or in Paradise, and the first is preferable. ﴿How excellent is the reward of the workers﴾; the object of praise is omitted, meaning: how excellent is the reward of the workers, their reward; and the meaning is: those who work at righteous deeds.

Then He described these workers, saying: ﴿Who are patient﴾ over the hardships of obligation and over the harm of the polytheists against them. It is permissible that it be accusative by way of praise. ﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾, that is: they entrust their affairs to Him in every undertaking and every withholding.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what aids patience and reliance, which is contemplating the condition of animals, saying: ﴿And how many a creature there is that carries not its provision; Allah provides for it and for you﴾. The discussion of ﹙ka'ayyin﹚ has already passed, and that its origin is ﹙ay﹚, the particle of comparison (ka) entered upon it, and in it came to mean "how many," as Khalil and Sibawayh stated explicitly; and its estimate according to both of them is "like a thing of many in number, of creatures."

It was also said: the meaning is: "and how many of creatures."

The meaning of ﹙la tahmilu rizqaha﹚ is: it cannot bear the carrying of its provision because of its weakness, nor does it store it. Rather Allah provides for it from His bounty, and provides for you. So how would they not rely upon Allah, despite their strength and their capability over the means of living, like its reliance upon Allah despite its weakness and incapacity?

al-Hasan said: It eats at its time; it stores nothing.

Mujahid said: It means birds and beasts eat with their mouths and carry nothing. And He is the All-Hearing who hears every thing heard, the All-Knowing of every thing known.

Then, glory be to Him, He mentioned the condition of the polytheists of Makkah and others, and the listener is astonished at their acknowledging that He is their Creator and their Provider, yet they do not affirm His oneness and abandon the worship of others. So He said: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth, and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ That is: He created them; they are not able to deny that, nor can they manage to reject it. ﴿So how are they turned away?﴾ That is: how are they diverted from acknowledging His singularity in divinity and that He alone has no partner? The interrogative is for denial and remoteness.

When the polytheists said to some of the believers, "If you were upon the truth you would not be poor," He, glory be to Him, repelled that with His saying: ﴿Allah extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants, and restricts it for him﴾; that is: the widening of provision and its straitening are from Allah, the Extender and the Restrainer; He extends it to whomever He wills and constricts it upon whomever He wills, according to what His wisdom requires and what befits the condition of His servants of restriction and extension. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, He knows what in it is the good of His servants and their corruption.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who sent down water from the sky and gave life thereby to the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah."﴾ That is: Allah sent it down and gave life thereby to the earth; they acknowledge that and find no way to deny it.

Then, since they made this acknowledgement in these verses, and it necessitates the falsehood of what they are upon of polytheism and of not singling out Allah, glory be to Him, in worship, He commanded His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, to praise Allah for their affirmation and their not denying, despite their stubbornness in obstinacy and their rigidity in rejecting everything the Messenger of Allah brought of monotheism. So He said: ﴿Say, "Praise be to Allah." But most of them do not reason﴾; that is: I praise Allah for making the truth with you and manifesting your proof against them. Then He censured them, saying: "Rather, most of them do not reason," the things that rational people reason.

Therefore they do not act in accordance with what they acknowledged, which necessitates the falsehood of what they are upon, in the view of every rational person.

Then, glory be to Him, He pointed to the belittling of this world and that it is of the nature of play and amusement, and that the true abode is the abode of the Hereafter, so He said: ﴿And this worldly life is not but amusement and play﴾, of the kind with which children amuse themselves and play; ﴿and indeed, the Home of the Hereafter — that is the [true] life﴾.

Ibn Qutaybah and Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-Hayawan is al-hayah (life).

al-Wahidi said: This is the view of all the exegetes; they held that the meaning of al-hayawan here is life, and that it is a verbal noun equivalent to al-hayah, like al-nazawan and al-ghalayan, and the estimate is: "and indeed the Home of the Hereafter is the home of al-hayawan," or "possessing al-hayawan," that is: the home of lasting life, which does not cease, and which is not troubled by death or sickness, nor by worry or grief. Had they known anything of knowledge, they would not have preferred over it the transient, troubled abode.

Then, glory be to Him, made clear that the sole obstacle preventing them from faith is not merely the influence of worldly life, so He said: ﴿So when they board the ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion﴾; that is: when their hope of life is cut off and they fear drowning, they return to the primordial nature, and they call upon Allah alone, being in the state of those sincere to Him in religion through the truthfulness of their intentions, and abandoning at that time the calling upon idols, knowing that none other than Allah, glory be to Him, can remove this great hardship that has descended upon them. ﴿But when He delivers them to land, at once they associate others with Him﴾; that is: they suddenly returned to polytheism and called upon other than Allah, glory be to Him.

Riding (ruku') is elevation, and it is transitive by itself; it was made transitive by the word "fi" only to indicate that what is ridden is itself of the category of places.

The lam in ﹙liyakfuru bima atainahum﹚ and in His saying ﹙waliyatamatta'u﹚ is for causation, meaning: they suddenly associate others with Allah, so that they may disbelieve in the blessing of Allah and so that they may enjoy both. Thus in the two verbs the lam is the lam of purpose. It was also said: both are imperative lams, for threat and warning: that is, "disbelieve in what We have given you of blessing, and enjoy," and the recitation of Ubayy, "wa-tamatta'u," supports this. This double possibility applies only to the reading of Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Warsh with a kasra on the lam; but on the reading of the majority with sukun, there is no disagreement that it is the lam of command. In His saying ﹙fasawfa ya'lamun﹚ there is a great threat to them, that is: they will soon know the outcome of that and the calamity upon them in it.

﴿Have they not seen that We made a sanctuary secure, while people are being taken from around them?﴾ That is: did they not look — meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh — that We made this their sanctuary a secure sanctuary, in which its inhabitant is safe from raiding, killing, captivity and plunder, so they were in safety and well-being from what others among the Arabs were in, for they are at every moment struck by raids, their wealth is seized by invaders, their blood is spilled by armies, and their sanctity and wealth are violated by the rogues and devils of the Arabs. The clause ﹙wa-yutakhatfu al-nas min hawlihim﹚ is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause, that is: they seize those around them by killing, captivity and plunder; and al-khatf is taking swiftly, and its verification has passed in Surat al-Qasas. ﴿Then in falsehood do they believe?﴾, which is polytheism after the manifestation of Allah's proof against them and their acknowledgement of what necessitates monotheism; ﴿and in the favour of Allah they deny?﴾, they make its disbelief in place of its thankfulness. In this interrogative is a rebuke and reproach beyond measure.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents about Allah a lie, or denies the truth when it has come to him?﴾ That is: none is more unjust than him, and he is one who claims that Allah has a partner; ﴿or denies the truth when it has come to him﴾, that is: denies the Messenger to whom he was sent and the Book that He sent down upon His Messenger.

Al-Suddi said: he denied monotheism; and the apparent meaning is that it includes whatever truly is the truth.

Then He threatened and warned the deniers, saying: ﴿Is there not in Hell a residence for the disbelievers?﴾, that is: a place in which they will settle. The interrogative is for affirmation, and the meaning is: do they not deserve to settle therein, since they have done what they have done?

Then, when He mentioned the condition of the polytheists who deny monotheism and disbelieve in the blessings of Allah, He followed it with the condition of His righteous servants, saying: ﴿And those who strive for Us — We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾; that is: they strive for the sake of Allah, seeking His pleasure and hoping for what is with Him of good, ﴿We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾, that is: the way that leads to Us.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is Makkan, descended before the obligation of conventional jihad; it is rather a general jihad in the religion of Allah and seeking His pleasure. It was also said: this verse was revealed concerning the worshippers. Ibrahim ibn Adham said: It is concerning those who act upon what they know. ﴿And indeed, Allah is with the doers of good﴾, with victory and help, and whoever is with Him is not forsaken. The emphatic lam entered upon ma'a under the interpretation that it is a noun, or on the basis that it is a particle, and the emphatic lam entered upon it to convey the meaning of permanence, as you say: "Indeed Zayd is in the house." The discussion is established in the science of grammar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

It has been related by Ibn Mardawayh, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾ [al-Zumar: 30], I said: 'O Lord, will all creation die while the prophets remain?' Then this was revealed: ﴿Every soul will taste death; then to Us you will be returned﴾" [al-'Ankabut: 57].

It should be examined how sound this is. After hearing the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, you will die, and indeed they will die﴾, the Prophet (ﷺ) knows that he will die, and he knows that the prophets before him have died, and that he is the Seal of the Prophets. So how could there arise from this verse what Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) asked about, namely his saying: "Will all creation die while the prophets remain?" It is therefore likely that this report is not sound, either as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) or as a mawquf (traced to a companion).

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn Asakir related, and al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain, from Ibn Umar, who said: "I went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) until he entered some of the orchards of Madinah, and he began to pick dates and eat. He said to me: 'Why do you not eat?' I said: 'I have no desire for it, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'But I have a desire for it, and this is the fourth morning since I last tasted food and did not find any. If I wished, I could supplicate my Lord and He would give me the like of the kingdom of Kisra and Caesar. So what will you do, O Ibn Umar, when you remain among a people who hoard the provision of their year and whose certainty weakens?'" He said: "By Allah, we did not move from there, nor did we depart, until there was revealed: ﴿And how many a creature does not carry its provision﴾, to the end of the verse. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed, Allah has not commanded me to hoard the world, nor to follow desires. Behold, I do not hoard a dinar or a dirham, nor do I store provision for tomorrow.'"

This hadith contains severe strangeness (nakarah), because it contradicts what the Prophet (ﷺ) practised. He used to give his wives the provision of a year, as is established in the reliable books of hadith.

In its chain is Abu al-'Atuf al-Jawzi, and he is weak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter is the [true] life﴾, that he said: "It is everlasting."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman related from Abu Ja'far, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "How strange, how very strange, is the one who believes in the abode of life while he strives for the abode of delusion." This is a mursal (a report in which the Successor omits the companion from the chain).

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verses 2–10 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1127) Ibn al-Darir, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il narrated through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Rum was revealed at Makkah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ahmad also narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a sound (hasan) chain from a man among the Companions: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the dawn prayer and recited in it Surat al-Rum." Al-Bazzar narrated the like of it from al-Aghharr al-Madani.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in the dawn prayer on Friday with Surat al-Rum." Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ahmad and Ibn Qani' narrated through the chain of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr the like of the hadith of the Companion man, and added: "He would hesitate in it. When he finished he said: 'Only people who attend the prayer without being in a state of purity confuse us in our prayer. Whoever attends the prayer, let him perform the purification well.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion of the opening of the surah has already preceded at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah, and the discussion of its grammatical position and the position of similar openings has already preceded in more than one place in the discussions of the openings of the surahs.

The majority recited ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾ ("The Romans have been defeated") with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam, in the passive voice. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it with a fathah on the ghayn and the lam, in the active voice.

Al-Nahhas said: the recitation of most people is "ghulibat" with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) said: Persia defeated the Romans, so the disbelievers of Makkah rejoiced at that and said: "Those who have no scripture have defeated those who have a scripture," and they boasted over the Muslims and said: "We too will defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans." The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were People of the Book.

The meaning of ﴿fi adna al-ard﴾ ("in the nearest land") is: in the land nearest to them from the land of the Arabs, or in the nearest land of the Arabs to them. It was said: it is the land of al-Jazirah; it was said: Adhri'at; it was said: Kaskar; it was said: al-Urdunn; it was said: Filastin. These places are closer to the lands of the Arabs than others. The "land" was taken to mean the land of the Arabs because it is what is familiar in their speech: when they say "the land" without qualification they mean the Arabian Peninsula. It was also said that the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement, and the implied meaning is: "in the nearest of their land," so the pronoun returns to the Romans, and the meaning becomes: "in the nearest land of the Romans to the Arabs."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: if the battle was at Adhri'at, then it is "the nearest land" measured from Makkah; if the battle was in al-Jazirah, then it is nearest measured from the land of Kisra; and if it was in al-Urdunn, then it is nearest to the land of the Romans.

﴿wa hum min ba'di ghalabihim sayaghlibun﴾ ("and they, after their defeat, will overcome") means: and the Romans, after the Persians defeated them, will overcome the people of Persia. "Ghalab" and "ghalabah" are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun. The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the object according to the recitation of the majority, and with the subject according to the recitation of others.

The majority recited "sayaghlibun" in the active voice, while 'Ali, Abu Sa'id, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it in the passive voice. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "min ba'di ghalbihim" with a sukun on the lam.

﴿fi bid' sinin﴾ ("within a few years") is connected to what precedes it. The explanation of "bid'" and its derivation has already preceded in Surat Yusuf, and what is meant by it here is between three and ten.

﴿lillahi al-amru min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ ("to Allah belongs the command, before and after") means: He alone holds power and the issuing of judgments, both at the time of their being defeated and at the time of their being victorious. All of that is by the command and decree of Allah, the Glorified.

The majority recited "min qablu wa min ba'du" with a dammah on both, because they are cut off from the genitive construction, and the implied meaning is: "from before the defeat and from after it," or "from before every matter and from after it."

Al-Kisa'i transmitted "min qablin wa min ba'du" with a kasrah on the first, nunated, and a dammah on the second, without nunation.

Al-Farra' transmitted "min qabli wa min ba'di" with kasrah on both, without nunation, and al-Nahhas considered this an error.

Shihab al-Din said: it has been recited with kasrah on both, nunated.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "from what precedes and from what follows."

﴿wa yawma'idhin yafrahu al-mu'minun bi-nasri Allah﴾ ("and on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah") means: on the day when the Romans overcome Persia after a few years, the believers will rejoice at Allah's victory for the Romans, because they are People of the Book just as the Muslims are People of the Book, unlike Persia, which has no scripture. For this reason the polytheists were pleased by the victory of the Persians over the Romans. It was said: the victory of Allah is the manifestation of the truthfulness of the believers in what they told the polytheists about the Romans' overcoming Persia; the first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is among the signs showing that the Qur'an is from Allah, because it is a report of what will happen, and no one knows this except Allah, the Glorified.

﴿yansuru man yasha'u an yansurahu wa huwa al-'Aziz al-Ghalib al-Qahir al-Rahim al-Kathir al-Rahmah li-'ibadihi al-mu'minin﴾ ("He grants victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Subduer, the Most Merciful, abundant in mercy to His believing servants"). It was said: the mercy here means worldly mercy, which includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever.

﴿wa'da Allah la yukhlifu Allah wa'dahu﴾ ("A promise of Allah; Allah does not fail His promise") means: Allah made a promise which He will not break, namely the victory of the Romans over Persia. ﴿wa lakinna aktara al-nasi la ya'lamun﴾ ("but most people do not know") means: they do not know that Allah does not break His promise. They are the disbelievers; it was said: specifically the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿ya'lamuna zahiran mina al-hayah al-dunya﴾ ("They know the outward of the worldly life") means: they know the outward aspect of what they see of the world's adornments and pleasures and the matters of their livelihood, (p-1128) and the means of obtaining their worldly benefits. It was said: it is what the devils convey to them of worldly matters when they eavesdrop on the heavens. It was said: "the outward" is falsehood, and they are heedless of the Hereafter, which is the everlasting blessing and pure delight, not turning to it nor preparing for it what is needed; or they are heedless of belief in it and of affirming its coming.

﴿awa lam yatafakkaru fi anfusihim ma khalaqa Allah al-samawati wa al-ard wa ma baynahuma﴾ ("Have they not reflected within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth") The hamzah is for rebuke against them, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element, as in its parallels. "Fi anfusihim" is an adverbial complement of the reflection, not its object. The meaning is: the causes of reflection are present for them, namely their own selves; if they reflected upon them as they should, they would know Allah's oneness and the truthfulness of His prophets. It was also said that it is the object of the reflection.

The meaning: have they not reflected upon Allah's creating them when they were nothing? "Ma" in "ma khalaqa Allah" is negative, meaning: He did not create them except with the established truth which is worthy of being established; or it is a noun in the accusative by omission of the preposition, meaning: "with what Allah created," and what governs it is either the knowledge which reflection leads to. Al-Zajjaj said there is an omission in the speech, meaning: "so that they would know," so he made "ma" the object of the implied verb, not of the knowledge implied. The "ba'" in "illa bil-haqq" is either causal, or it and its genitive are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: "accompanied by truth."

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "illa li-l-haqq," i.e., for the reward and punishment. It was said: "bil-haqq" means "with justice"; it was said: "with wisdom"; it was said: "bil-haqq" meaning that He is the Truth and created them for the Truth.

"Wa ajalin musamman" is conjoined to "al-haqq": that is, and with a specified term for the heavens and the earth and what is between them, at which they end, and it is the Day of Resurrection. In this is an alert to annihilation, and that every created thing has a term it does not exceed.

It was said: the meaning of "wa ajalin musamman" is that He created what He created at a time He designated for the creation of that thing.

﴿wa inna kathiran mina al-nasi bi-liqa'i rabbihim la-kafirun﴾ ("Indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord") means: disbelievers in the resurrection after death. The "lam" is the emphatic lam. By "these" is meant the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿awa lam yasiru fi al-ard﴾ ("Have they not traveled through the land") The interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, because they did not reflect upon the traces and did not contemplate the places of lessons. The fa' in "fa-yandhuru" is conjoined to "yasiru" and falls under what the interrogative includes of reproach and rebuke. The meaning: they have traveled and witnessed ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾ of the groups of disbelievers whom Allah destroyed because of their disbelief in Allah, their denial of the truth, and their denial of the messengers. The clause ﴿they were stronger than them in power﴾ explains the manner in which they were, and that they were more capable than the disbelievers of Makkah and those who followed them in worldly matters. The meaning of ﴿they tilled the earth﴾ is they plowed it and turned it over for cultivation and pursued the means of that, and the people of Makkah were not people of tillage. ﴿and they populated it more than these have populated it﴾ means: they populated it with a population greater than these people did, because those were longer-lived than them, stronger in bodies, and more abundant in acquiring the means of livelihood.

So they populated the earth with buildings, cultivation and planting. ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., miracles; it was said: with the legal rulings. ﴿Allah would not wrong them by punishing them without sin, but they were wronging themselves by disbelief and denial.﴾

﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst﴾ means: those who committed evil deeds of polytheism and sins. "Al-su'a" is the feminine form of "al-asw'a," meaning the most evil; i.e., their end was the punishment which is the worst of punishments. It was said: it is the name of Hell, just as "al-husna" is the name of Paradise. It may be a verbal noun like "al-bushra" and "al-dhikra." The punishment is described with it for emphasis.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "'aqibatu" with a dammah as the subject of "kana," and the verb is masculine because its feminine marking is metaphorical; the predicate is "al-su'a," i.e., the deed or the trait or the punishment that is worst. Or the predicate is "an kadhdhabu," meaning: their last affair was denial, the end of those who did evil. "Al-su'a" is the verbal noun of "asa'u" or an adjective of an omitted noun.

Al-Kisa'i said: "an kadhdhabu" is in the accusative position as a causal clause, meaning: because they denied the signs of Allah which He sent down upon His messengers, or "bi-an kadhdhabu." Among those who say that "al-su'a" is Hell are al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah and most of the exegetes, and it was called "su'a" because it causes its companion distress.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: then the end of those who associated partners with Allah was the Fire, because of their denial of the signs of Allah and their mockery. The clause ﴿and they used to mock at them﴾ is conjoined to "kadhdhabu," and falls together with it under the causal sense according to one view, or under the nominal sense of "kana," or the predicative sense of it according to the other view.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾, that he said: "The polytheists used to love that Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they were people of idols, and the Muslims used to love that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were people of a scripture. They mentioned that to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Indeed they will overcome.' Abu Bakr mentioned it to them, and they said: 'Set between us and you a term; if we prevail, we will have such and such, and if you prevail, you will have such and such.' So he set a term between them of five years, and they did not prevail. Abu Bakr mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it—I think he said—fewer than ten?' Then the Romans prevailed after that, and that is His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾, so they were defeated, then they were defeated again after that by the saying of Allah: ﴿To Allah belongs the command, before and after. And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾."

Sufyan said: I heard that they prevailed over them on the day of Badr.

It was narrated by Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, with a similar report, and he added that when the term had passed and the Romans had not overcome the Persians, the Prophet (ﷺ) was displeased with what Abu Bakr had set as the period and disliked it, and said: "What prompted you to this?" He said: "Affirmation of God and His Messenger." So he (ﷺ) said: "Go back to them, raise the stakes, and make it a few years." So Abu Bakr went to them and said: "Are you willing to return to the wager? For returning is more commendable." They said: "Yes." Those years had not passed before the Romans overcame the Persians, and they tied their horses in al-Mada'in and built Rumiyya. Abu Bakr won the wager and brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "This is ill-gotten gain (suḥt); give it in charity."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated on the authority of Niyar ibn Mukram al-Aslami, who said: When the verses ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The Byzantines have been defeated﴾ were revealed, the Persians were at that time, the day this verse was revealed, victorious over the Romans. The Muslims loved the Romans to prevail over them, because they and the Romans were People of the Book. Concerning this God says: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in God's victory﴾. So when God revealed this verse, Abu Bakr went out crying in the outskirts of Mecca: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verses 2–10 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ahmad also narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a sound (hasan) chain from a man among the Companions: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the dawn prayer and recited in it Surat al-Rum." Al-Bazzar narrated the like of it from al-Aghharr al-Madani.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in the dawn prayer on Friday with Surat al-Rum." Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ahmad and Ibn Qani' narrated through the chain of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr the like of the hadith of the Companion man, and added: "He would hesitate in it. When he finished he said: 'Only people who attend the prayer without being in a state of purity confuse us in our prayer. Whoever attends the prayer, let him perform the purification well.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion of the opening of the surah has already preceded at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah, and the discussion of its grammatical position and the position of similar openings has already preceded in more than one place in the discussions of the openings of the surahs.

The majority recited ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾ ("The Romans have been defeated") with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam, in the passive voice. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it with a fathah on the ghayn and the lam, in the active voice.

Al-Nahhas said: the recitation of most people is "ghulibat" with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) said: Persia defeated the Romans, so the disbelievers of Makkah rejoiced at that and said: "Those who have no scripture have defeated those who have a scripture," and they boasted over the Muslims and said: "We too will defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans." The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were People of the Book.

The meaning of ﴿fi adna al-ard﴾ ("in the nearest land") is: in the land nearest to them from the land of the Arabs, or in the nearest land of the Arabs to them. It was said: it is the land of al-Jazirah; it was said: Adhri'at; it was said: Kaskar; it was said: al-Urdunn; it was said: Filastin. These places are closer to the lands of the Arabs than others. The "land" was taken to mean the land of the Arabs because it is what is familiar in their speech: when they say "the land" without qualification they mean the Arabian Peninsula. It was also said that the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement, and the implied meaning is: "in the nearest of their land," so the pronoun returns to the Romans, and the meaning becomes: "in the nearest land of the Romans to the Arabs."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: if the battle was at Adhri'at, then it is "the nearest land" measured from Makkah; if the battle was in al-Jazirah, then it is nearest measured from the land of Kisra; and if it was in al-Urdunn, then it is nearest to the land of the Romans.

﴿wa hum min ba'di ghalabihim sayaghlibun﴾ ("and they, after their defeat, will overcome") means: and the Romans, after the Persians defeated them, will overcome the people of Persia. "Ghalab" and "ghalabah" are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun. The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the object according to the recitation of the majority, and with the subject according to the recitation of others.

The majority recited "sayaghlibun" in the active voice, while 'Ali, Abu Sa'id, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it in the passive voice. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "min ba'di ghalbihim" with a sukun on the lam.

﴿fi bid' sinin﴾ ("within a few years") is connected to what precedes it. The explanation of "bid'" and its derivation has already preceded in Surat Yusuf, and what is meant by it here is between three and ten.

﴿lillahi al-amru min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ ("to Allah belongs the command, before and after") means: He alone holds power and the issuing of judgments, both at the time of their being defeated and at the time of their being victorious. All of that is by the command and decree of Allah, the Glorified.

The majority recited "min qablu wa min ba'du" with a dammah on both, because they are cut off from the genitive construction, and the implied meaning is: "from before the defeat and from after it," or "from before every matter and from after it."

Al-Kisa'i transmitted "min qablin wa min ba'du" with a kasrah on the first, nunated, and a dammah on the second, without nunation.

Al-Farra' transmitted "min qabli wa min ba'di" with kasrah on both, without nunation, and al-Nahhas considered this an error.

Shihab al-Din said: it has been recited with kasrah on both, nunated.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "from what precedes and from what follows."

﴿wa yawma'idhin yafrahu al-mu'minun bi-nasri Allah﴾ ("and on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah") means: on the day when the Romans overcome Persia after a few years, the believers will rejoice at Allah's victory for the Romans, because they are People of the Book just as the Muslims are People of the Book, unlike Persia, which has no scripture. For this reason the polytheists were pleased by the victory of the Persians over the Romans. It was said: the victory of Allah is the manifestation of the truthfulness of the believers in what they told the polytheists about the Romans' overcoming Persia; the first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is among the signs showing that the Qur'an is from Allah, because it is a report of what will happen, and no one knows this except Allah, the Glorified.

﴿yansuru man yasha'u an yansurahu wa huwa al-'Aziz al-Ghalib al-Qahir al-Rahim al-Kathir al-Rahmah li-'ibadihi al-mu'minin﴾ ("He grants victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Subduer, the Most Merciful, abundant in mercy to His believing servants"). It was said: the mercy here means worldly mercy, which includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever.

﴿wa'da Allah la yukhlifu Allah wa'dahu﴾ ("A promise of Allah; Allah does not fail His promise") means: Allah made a promise which He will not break, namely the victory of the Romans over Persia. ﴿wa lakinna aktara al-nasi la ya'lamun﴾ ("but most people do not know") means: they do not know that Allah does not break His promise. They are the disbelievers; it was said: specifically the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿ya'lamuna zahiran mina al-hayah al-dunya﴾ ("They know the outward of the worldly life") means: they know the outward aspect of what they see of the world's adornments and pleasures and the matters of their livelihood, (p-1128) and the means of obtaining their worldly benefits. It was said: it is what the devils convey to them of worldly matters when they eavesdrop on the heavens. It was said: "the outward" is falsehood, and they are heedless of the Hereafter, which is the everlasting blessing and pure delight, not turning to it nor preparing for it what is needed; or they are heedless of belief in it and of affirming its coming.

﴿awa lam yatafakkaru fi anfusihim ma khalaqa Allah al-samawati wa al-ard wa ma baynahuma﴾ ("Have they not reflected within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth") The hamzah is for rebuke against them, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element, as in its parallels. "Fi anfusihim" is an adverbial complement of the reflection, not its object. The meaning is: the causes of reflection are present for them, namely their own selves; if they reflected upon them as they should, they would know Allah's oneness and the truthfulness of His prophets. It was also said that it is the object of the reflection.

Al-Zajjaj said there is an omission in the speech, meaning: "so that they would know," so he made "ma" the object of the implied verb, not of the knowledge implied. The "ba'" in "illa bil-haqq" is either causal, or it and its genitive are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: "accompanied by truth."

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "illa li-l-haqq," i.e., for the reward and punishment. It was said: "bil-haqq" means "with justice"; it was said: "with wisdom"; it was said: "bil-haqq" meaning that He is the Truth and created them for the Truth.

"Wa ajalin musamman" is conjoined to "al-haqq": that is, and with a specified term for the heavens and the earth and what is between them, at which they end, and it is the Day of Resurrection. In this is an alert to annihilation, and that every created thing has a term it does not exceed.

It was said: the meaning of "wa ajalin musamman" is that He created what He created at a time He designated for the creation of that thing.

﴿wa inna kathiran mina al-nasi bi-liqa'i rabbihim la-kafirun﴾ ("Indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord") means: disbelievers in the resurrection after death. The "lam" is the emphatic lam. By "these" is meant the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah.

The fa' in "fa-yandhuru" is conjoined to "yasiru" and falls under what the interrogative includes of reproach and rebuke. The meaning: they have traveled and witnessed ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾ of the groups of disbelievers whom Allah destroyed because of their disbelief in Allah, their denial of the truth, and their denial of the messengers. The clause ﴿they were stronger than them in power﴾ explains the manner in which they were, and that they were more capable than the disbelievers of Makkah and those who followed them in worldly matters. The meaning of ﴿they tilled the earth﴾ is they plowed it and turned it over for cultivation and pursued the means of that, and the people of Makkah were not people of tillage. ﴿and they populated it more than these have populated it﴾ means: they populated it with a population greater than these people did, because those were longer-lived than them, stronger in bodies, and more abundant in acquiring the means of livelihood.

So they populated the earth with buildings, cultivation and planting. ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., miracles; it was said: with the legal rulings. ﴿Allah would not wrong them by punishing them without sin, but they were wronging themselves by disbelief and denial.﴾

Al-Nahhas said: the recitation of most people is "ghulibat" with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) said: Persia defeated the Romans, so the disbelievers of Makkah rejoiced at that and said: "Those who have no scripture have defeated those who have a scripture," and they boasted over the Muslims and said: "We too will defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans." The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were People of the Book.

The meaning of ﴿fi adna al-ard﴾ ("in the nearest land") is: in the land nearest to them from the land of the Arabs, or in the nearest land of the Arabs to them. It was said: it is the land of al-Jazirah; it was said: Adhri'at; it was said: Kaskar; it was said: al-Urdunn; it was said: Filastin. These places are closer to the lands of the Arabs than others. The "land" was taken to mean the land of the Arabs because it is what is familiar in their speech: when they say "the land" without qualification they mean the Arabian Peninsula. It was also said that the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement, and the implied meaning is: "in the nearest of their land," so the pronoun returns to the Romans, and the meaning becomes: "in the nearest land of the Romans to the Arabs."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: if the battle was at Adhri'at, then it is "the nearest land" measured from Makkah; if the battle was in al-Jazirah, then it is nearest measured from the land of Kisra; and if it was in al-Urdunn, then it is nearest to the land of the Romans.

﴿wa hum min ba'di ghalabihim sayaghlibun﴾ ("and they, after their defeat, will overcome") means: and the Romans, after the Persians defeated them, will overcome the people of Persia. "Ghalab" and "ghalabah" are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun. The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the object according to the recitation of the majority, and with the subject according to the recitation of others.

The majority recited "sayaghlibun" in the active voice, while 'Ali, Abu Sa'id, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it in the passive voice. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "min ba'di ghalbihim" with a sukun on the lam.

﴿fi bid' sinin﴾ ("within a few years") is connected to what precedes it. The explanation of "bid'" and its derivation has already preceded in Surat Yusuf, and what is meant by it here is between three and ten.

﴿lillahi al-amru min qablu wa min ba'du﴾ ("to Allah belongs the command, before and after") means: He alone holds power and the issuing of judgments, both at the time of their being defeated and at the time of their being victorious. All of that is by the command and decree of Allah, the Glorified.

The majority recited "min qablu wa min ba'du" with a dammah on both, because they are cut off from the genitive construction, and the implied meaning is: "from before the defeat and from after it," or "from before every matter and from after it."

Al-Kisa'i transmitted "min qablin wa min ba'du" with a kasrah on the first, nunated, and a dammah on the second, without nunation.

Al-Farra' transmitted "min qabli wa min ba'di" with kasrah on both, without nunation, and al-Nahhas considered this an error.

Shihab al-Din said: it has been recited with kasrah on both, nunated.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "from what precedes and from what follows."

﴿wa yawma'idhin yafrahu al-mu'minun bi-nasri Allah﴾ ("and on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah") means: on the day when the Romans overcome Persia after a few years, the believers will rejoice at Allah's victory for the Romans, because they are People of the Book just as the Muslims are People of the Book, unlike Persia, which has no scripture. For this reason the polytheists were pleased by the victory of the Persians over the Romans. It was said: the victory of Allah is the manifestation of the truthfulness of the believers in what they told the polytheists about the Romans' overcoming Persia; the first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is among the signs showing that the Qur'an is from Allah, because it is a report of what will happen, and no one knows this except Allah, the Glorified.

﴿yansuru man yasha'u an yansurahu wa huwa al-'Aziz al-Ghalib al-Qahir al-Rahim al-Kathir al-Rahmah li-'ibadihi al-mu'minin﴾ ("He grants victory to whom He wills, and He is the Mighty, the Overpowering, the Subduer, the Most Merciful, abundant in mercy to His believing servants"). It was said: the mercy here means worldly mercy, which includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever.

﴿wa'da Allah la yukhlifu Allah wa'dahu﴾ ("A promise of Allah; Allah does not fail His promise") means: Allah made a promise which He will not break, namely the victory of the Romans over Persia. ﴿wa lakinna aktara al-nasi la ya'lamun﴾ ("but most people do not know") means: they do not know that Allah does not break His promise. They are the disbelievers; it was said: specifically the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿ya'lamuna zahiran mina al-hayah al-dunya﴾ ("They know the outward of the worldly life") means: they know the outward aspect of what they see of the world's adornments and pleasures and the matters of their livelihood, (p-1128) and the means of obtaining their worldly benefits. It was said: it is what the devils convey to them of worldly matters when they eavesdrop on the heavens. It was said: "the outward" is falsehood, and they are heedless of the Hereafter, which is the everlasting blessing and pure delight, not turning to it nor preparing for it what is needed; or they are heedless of belief in it and of affirming its coming.

﴿awa lam yatafakkaru fi anfusihim ma khalaqa Allah al-samawati wa al-ard wa ma baynahuma﴾ ("Have they not reflected within themselves? Allah did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth") The hamzah is for rebuke against them, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied element, as in its parallels. "Fi anfusihim" is an adverbial complement of the reflection, not its object. The meaning is: the causes of reflection are present for them, namely their own selves; if they reflected upon them as they should, they would know Allah's oneness and the truthfulness of His prophets. It was also said that it is the object of the reflection.

The meaning: have they not reflected upon Allah's creating them when they were nothing? "Ma" in "ma khalaqa Allah" is negative, meaning: He did not create them except with the established truth which is worthy of being established; or it is a noun in the accusative by omission of the preposition, meaning: "with what Allah created," and what governs it is either the knowledge which reflection leads to. Al-Zajjaj said there is an omission in the speech, meaning: "so that they would know," so he made "ma" the object of the implied verb, not of the knowledge implied. The "ba'" in "illa bil-haqq" is either causal, or it and its genitive are in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, meaning: "accompanied by truth."

Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "illa li-l-haqq," i.e., for the reward and punishment. It was said: "bil-haqq" means "with justice"; it was said: "with wisdom"; it was said: "bil-haqq" meaning that He is the Truth and created them for the Truth.

"Wa ajalin musamman" is conjoined to "al-haqq": that is, and with a specified term for the heavens and the earth and what is between them, at which they end, and it is the Day of Resurrection. In this is an alert to annihilation, and that every created thing has a term it does not exceed.

It was said: the meaning of "wa ajalin musamman" is that He created what He created at a time He designated for the creation of that thing.

﴿wa inna kathiran mina al-nasi bi-liqa'i rabbihim la-kafirun﴾ ("Indeed, many of the people are disbelievers in the meeting with their Lord") means: disbelievers in the resurrection after death. The "lam" is the emphatic lam. By "these" is meant the disbelievers in general, or the disbelievers of Makkah.

﴿awa lam yasiru fi al-ard﴾ ("Have they not traveled through the land") The interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, because they did not reflect upon the traces and did not contemplate the places of lessons. The fa' in "fa-yandhuru" is conjoined to "yasiru" and falls under what the interrogative includes of reproach and rebuke. The meaning: they have traveled and witnessed ﴿how was the end of those before them﴾ of the groups of disbelievers whom Allah destroyed because of their disbelief in Allah, their denial of the truth, and their denial of the messengers. The clause ﴿they were stronger than them in power﴾ explains the manner in which they were, and that they were more capable than the disbelievers of Makkah and those who followed them in worldly matters. The meaning of ﴿they tilled the earth﴾ is they plowed it and turned it over for cultivation and pursued the means of that, and the people of Makkah were not people of tillage. ﴿and they populated it more than these have populated it﴾ means: they populated it with a population greater than these people did, because those were longer-lived than them, stronger in bodies, and more abundant in acquiring the means of livelihood.

So they populated the earth with buildings, cultivation and planting. ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, i.e., miracles; it was said: with the legal rulings. ﴿Allah would not wrong them by punishing them without sin, but they were wronging themselves by disbelief and denial.﴾

﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst﴾ means: those who committed evil deeds of polytheism and sins. "Al-su'a" is the feminine form of "al-asw'a," meaning the most evil; i.e., their end was the punishment which is the worst of punishments. It was said: it is the name of Hell, just as "al-husna" is the name of Paradise. It may be a verbal noun like "al-bushra" and "al-dhikra." The punishment is described with it for emphasis.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "'aqibatu" with a dammah as the subject of "kana," and the verb is masculine because its feminine marking is metaphorical; the predicate is "al-su'a," i.e., the deed or the trait or the punishment that is worst. Or the predicate is "an kadhdhabu," meaning: their last affair was denial, the end of those who did evil. "Al-su'a" is the verbal noun of "asa'u" or an adjective of an omitted noun.

Al-Kisa'i said: "an kadhdhabu" is in the accusative position as a causal clause, meaning: because they denied the signs of Allah which He sent down upon His messengers, or "bi-an kadhdhabu." Among those who say that "al-su'a" is Hell are al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah and most of the exegetes, and it was called "su'a" because it causes its companion distress.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: then the end of those who associated partners with Allah was the Fire, because of their denial of the signs of Allah and their mockery. The clause ﴿and they used to mock at them﴾ is conjoined to "kadhdhabu," and falls together with it under the causal sense according to one view, or under the nominal sense of "kana," or the predicative sense of it according to the other view.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾, that he said: "The polytheists used to love that Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they were people of idols, and the Muslims used to love that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were people of a scripture. They mentioned that to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Indeed they will overcome.' Abu Bakr mentioned it to them, and they said: 'Set between us and you a term; if we prevail, we will have such and such, and if you prevail, you will have such and such.' So he set a term between them of five years, and they did not prevail. Abu Bakr mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it—I think he said—fewer than ten?' Then the Romans prevailed after that, and that is His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾, so they were defeated, then they were defeated again after that by the saying of Allah: ﴿To Allah belongs the command, before and after. And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾."

Sufyan said: I heard that they prevailed over them on the day of Badr.

It was narrated by Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, with a similar report, and he added that when the term had passed and the Romans had not overcome the Persians, the Prophet (ﷺ) was displeased with what Abu Bakr had set as the period and disliked it, and said: "What prompted you to this?" He said: "Affirmation of God and His Messenger." So he (ﷺ) said: "Go back to them, raise the stakes, and make it a few years." So Abu Bakr went to them and said: "Are you willing to return to the wager? For returning is more commendable." They said: "Yes." Those years had not passed before the Romans overcame the Persians, and they tied their horses in al-Mada'in and built Rumiyya. Abu Bakr won the wager and brought it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he said: "This is ill-gotten gain (suḥt); give it in charity."

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (ṣaḥīḥ), al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym in al-Dala'il, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated on the authority of Niyar ibn Mukram al-Aslami, who said: When the verses ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿The Byzantines have been defeated﴾ were revealed, the Persians were at that time, the day this verse was revealed, victorious over the Romans. The Muslims loved the Romans to prevail over them, because they and the Romans were People of the Book. Concerning this God says: ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice in God's victory﴾. Quraysh loved the Persians to prevail, because they and the Persians were not People of the Book, nor believers in resurrection. So when God revealed this verse, Abu Bakr went out crying in the outskirts of Mecca: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Byzantines have been defeated in the nearest land, but they, after their defeat, will overcome within a few years﴾. Some men of Quraysh said to Abu Bakr: "That is between us and you. Your companion claims that the Romans will overcome the Persians within a few years. Shall we not wager with you on that?" He said: "Yes, and that was before the prohibition of wagering." Abu Bakr and the polytheists placed their stakes and agreed on the wager. They said to Abu Bakr: "You did not make the few years three up to nine, so set between us and you a middle limit to which it will end." He said: "They set between them six years." Six years passed before they prevailed, so the polytheists took Abu Bakr's stake. When the seventh year came, the Romans prevailed. The Muslims blamed Abu Bakr for setting six years, because God said ﴿within a few years﴾. At that point many people embraced Islam.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good (ḥasan), and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr: "Why did you not reduce it, O Abu Bakr? For the few (bid') is between three and nine."

Al-Bukhari narrated a similar report from him in his History.

Al-Firyabi, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Abu Sa'id, who said: When it was the day of Badr, the Romans prevailed over the Persians, and that pleased the believers. So the verses were revealed: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. The Byzantines have been defeated﴾ he recited it with a fatha on the ghayn (ghalabat, with the verb in the active sense), meaning, to the words ﴿the believers will rejoice in God's victory﴾.

He said: So the believers rejoiced at the Romans' victory over the Persians. This report explains the recitation of Abu Sa'id and those with him.

Al-Hakim, who authenticated it (ṣaḥīḥ), narrated on the authority of Abu al-Darda', who said: "There will come peoples who will recite 'Alif, Lam, Mim, ghalabat al-Rum' meaning with a fatha on the ghayn, whereas it is ghulibat, meaning with a ḍamma on it." There are other reports on this matter, and what we have mentioned suffices from them.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾, meaning their livelihoods: when they plant, and when they sow, and when they harvest.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn 'Umar concerning God's words ﴿They were stronger than them in power﴾, that he said: A man among those before you had a span between his shoulders.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verses 2–10 (part 1 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated the like of it from Ibn al-Zubayr. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ahmad also narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a sound (hasan) chain from a man among the Companions: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the dawn prayer and recited in it Surat al-Rum." Al-Bazzar narrated the like of it from al-Aghharr al-Madani.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in the dawn prayer on Friday with Surat al-Rum." Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ahmad and Ibn Qani' narrated through the chain of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr the like of the hadith of the Companion man, and added: "He would hesitate in it. When he finished he said: 'Only people who attend the prayer without being in a state of purity confuse us in our prayer. Whoever attends the prayer, let him perform the purification well.'"

﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst﴾ means: those who committed evil deeds of polytheism and sins. "Al-su'a" is the feminine form of "al-asw'a," meaning the most evil; i.e., their end was the punishment which is the worst of punishments. It was said: it is the name of Hell, just as "al-husna" is the name of Paradise. It may be a verbal noun like "al-bushra" and "al-dhikra." The punishment is described with it for emphasis.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "'aqibatu" with a dammah as the subject of "kana," and the verb is masculine because its feminine marking is metaphorical; the predicate is "al-su'a," i.e., the deed or the trait or the punishment that is worst. Or the predicate is "an kadhdhabu," meaning: their last affair was denial, the end of those who did evil. "Al-su'a" is the verbal noun of "asa'u" or an adjective of an omitted noun.

Al-Kisa'i said: "an kadhdhabu" is in the accusative position as a causal clause, meaning: because they denied the signs of Allah which He sent down upon His messengers, or "bi-an kadhdhabu." Among those who say that "al-su'a" is Hell are al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutaybah and most of the exegetes, and it was called "su'a" because it causes its companion distress.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: then the end of those who associated partners with Allah was the Fire, because of their denial of the signs of Allah and their mockery. The clause ﴿and they used to mock at them﴾ is conjoined to "kadhdhabu," and falls together with it under the causal sense according to one view, or under the nominal sense of "kana," or the predicative sense of it according to the other view.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan), al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Kabir, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾, that he said: "The polytheists used to love that Persia would prevail over the Romans, because they were people of idols, and the Muslims used to love that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were people of a scripture. They mentioned that to Abu Bakr, and Abu Bakr mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Indeed they will overcome.' Abu Bakr mentioned it to them, and they said: 'Set between us and you a term; if we prevail, we will have such and such, and if you prevail, you will have such and such.' So he set a term between them of five years, and they did not prevail. Abu Bakr mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: 'Why did you not make it—I think he said—fewer than ten?' Then the Romans prevailed after that, and that is His saying: ﴿Alif Lam Mim﴾ ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾, so they were defeated, then they were defeated again after that by the saying of Allah: ﴿To Allah belongs the command, before and after. And on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah﴾."

Sufyan said: I heard that they prevailed over them on the day of Badr.

It was narrated by Abu Ya'la, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir, on the authority of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, with a similar report, and he added that when the term had passed and the Romans had not overcome the Persians, the Prophet (ﷺ) was displeased with what Abu Bakr had set as the period and disliked it, and said: "What prompted you to this?" He said: "Affirmation of God and His Messenger." So he (ﷺ) said: "Go back to them, raise the stakes, and make it a few years." So Abu Bakr went to them and said: "Are you willing to return to the wager? For returning is more commendable." They said: "Yes." Those years had not passed before the Romans overcame the Persians, and they tied their horses in al-Mada'in and built Rumiyya. 'Abd al-Razzaq and Ahmad also narrated, and al-Suyuti said with a sound (hasan) chain from a man among the Companions: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led them in the dawn prayer and recited in it Surat al-Rum." Al-Bazzar narrated the like of it from al-Aghharr al-Madani.

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr that "the Prophet (ﷺ) recited in the dawn prayer on Friday with Surat al-Rum." Ibn Abi Shaybah in al-Musannaf, Ahmad and Ibn Qani' narrated through the chain of 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr the like of the hadith of the Companion man, and added: "He would hesitate in it. When he finished he said: 'Only people who attend the prayer without being in a state of purity confuse us in our prayer. Whoever attends the prayer, let him perform the purification well.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The discussion of the opening of the surah has already preceded at the opening of Surat al-Baqarah, and the discussion of its grammatical position and the position of similar openings has already preceded in more than one place in the discussions of the openings of the surahs.

The majority recited ﴿Ghulibat al-Rum﴾ ("The Romans have been defeated") with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam, in the passive voice. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it with a fathah on the ghayn and the lam, in the active voice.

Al-Nahhas said: the recitation of most people is "ghulibat" with a dammah on the ghayn and a kasrah on the lam.

The people of tafsir (ahl al-tafsir) said: Persia defeated the Romans, so the disbelievers of Makkah rejoiced at that and said: "Those who have no scripture have defeated those who have a scripture," and they boasted over the Muslims and said: "We too will defeat you just as Persia defeated the Romans." The Muslims loved that the Romans would prevail over Persia because they were People of the Book.

The meaning of ﴿fi adna al-ard﴾ ("in the nearest land") is: in the land nearest to them from the land of the Arabs, or in the nearest land of the Arabs to them. It was said: it is the land of al-Jazirah; it was said: Adhri'at; it was said: Kaskar; it was said: al-Urdunn; it was said: Filastin. These places are closer to the lands of the Arabs than others. The "land" was taken to mean the land of the Arabs because it is what is familiar in their speech: when they say "the land" without qualification they mean the Arabian Peninsula. It was also said that the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement, and the implied meaning is: "in the nearest of their land," so the pronoun returns to the Romans, and the meaning becomes: "in the nearest land of the Romans to the Arabs."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: if the battle was at Adhri'at, then it is "the nearest land" measured from Makkah; if the battle was in al-Jazirah, then it is nearest measured from the land of Kisra; and if it was in al-Urdunn, then it is nearest to the land of the Romans.

﴿wa hum min ba'di ghalabihim sayaghlibun﴾ ("and they, after their defeat, will overcome") means: and the Romans, after the Persians defeated them, will overcome the people of Persia. "Ghalab" and "ghalabah" are two dialectal forms of the verbal noun. The verbal noun is in the genitive construction with the object according to the recitation of the majority, and with the subject according to the recitation of others.

The majority recited "sayaghlibun" in the active voice, while 'Ali, Abu Sa'id, Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, Ibn 'Umar and the people of Syria recited it in the passive voice. Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "min ba'di ghalbihim" with a sukun on the lam.

Al-Kisa'i transmitted "min qablin wa min ba'du" with a kasrah on the first, nunated, and a dammah on the second, without nunation.

Al-Farra' transmitted "min qabli wa min ba'di" with kasrah on both, without nunation, and al-Nahhas considered this an error.

Shihab al-Din said: it has been recited with kasrah on both, nunated.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of the verse is: "from what precedes and from what follows."

﴿wa yawma'idhin yafrahu al-mu'minun bi-nasri Allah﴾ ("and on that day the believers will rejoice in the victory of Allah") means: on the day when the Romans overcome Persia after a few years, the believers will rejoice at Allah's victory for the Romans, because they are People of the Book just as the Muslims are People of the Book, unlike Persia, which has no scripture. For this reason the polytheists were pleased by the victory of the Persians over the Romans. It was said: the victory of Allah is the manifestation of the truthfulness of the believers in what they told the polytheists about the Romans' overcoming Persia; the first view is preferable.

Al-Zajjaj said: this verse is among the signs showing that the Qur'an is from Allah, because it is a report of what will happen, and no one knows this except Allah, the Glorified.

It was said: the mercy here means worldly mercy, which includes both the Muslim and the disbeliever.

They are the disbelievers; it was said: specifically the disbelievers of Makkah.

It was said: it is what the devils convey to them of worldly matters when they eavesdrop on the heavens.
