Then, when He had explained the end of the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, He guided the believers to that which contains abundant reward and general good.

He said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. The fa' (so) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, that is: when you know that, then glorify Allah, that is, declare Him free of what is unfitting for Him, in the time of morning and evening, and in the afternoon and at midday.

It was said: what is meant by tasbih here is the five daily prayers. So His saying "when you enter the evening" is the prayers of maghrib and 'isha', His saying "and when you enter the morning" is the prayer of fajr, His saying "and in the afternoon" is the prayer of 'asr, and His saying "when you reach midday" is the prayer of zuhr. Thus said al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others.

al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: the meaning of "so glorify Allah" is "so pray to Allah."

al-Nahhas said: the people of tafsir hold that this verse concerns the prayers. He said: I heard Muhammad ibn Zayd say: its reality, in my view, is "so glorify Allah in the prayers," because glorification occurs in prayer. The clause ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'tarida, interjected between parts of a sentence), brought to guide to praise and to indicate the legitimacy of combining it with glorification, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾ [al-Hijr: 98] and His saying: ﴿while we glorify with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. It was said: the meaning of "and to Him belongs praise" is the exclusivity to Him of the prayer in which praise is recited. The first is preferable.

Ikrimah recited "hinan tumsuna wa hinan tusbihuna" (at a time when you enter the evening and at a time when you enter the morning). The meaning is: at a time when you enter the evening in it and at a time when you enter the morning in it. "Al-'ashiyy" (the evening) runs from the maghrib prayer to the 'atamah (the late night). Al-Jawhari said this. Others said: it runs from the decline of the sun to the rising of dawn. From this is the saying of the poet:

"We set out at dawn, in the pre-dawn darkness of the night,
and in the evening, after the middle of the day had passed."

His saying "'ashiyyan" (in the afternoon) is conjoined to "hina" (at a time). "In the heavens and the earth" is connected to the praise itself, that is: the praise to Him takes place in the heavens and the earth.

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, like the human from the sperm-drop, and the bird from the egg; ﴿and He brings the dead out of the living﴾, like the sperm-drop and the egg from the animal.

The explanation of this has already passed in the surah of Al 'Imran.

It was said: the connection of this verse with the preceding one is that a person, at morning, emerges from a semblance of death, which is sleep, into a semblance of existence, which is wakefulness; and at night he emerges from wakefulness into sleep. ﴿And He revives the earth after its death﴾, that is, He revives it with plants after its death by dryness. This is similar to bringing the living out of the dead. ﴿And thus you will be brought out﴾, that is, like that bringing out you will be brought out of your graves.

The majority recited "tukhrajun" (you will be brought out) in the passive voice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it in the active voice, attributing the going out to them, as in His saying: ﴿On the day they come forth from the graves﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43].

﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, that is, among His dazzling signs that indicate the resurrection is that He created you, that is, created your father Adam from dust, and created you within His creation of him, because the branch is drawn from the root and taken from it. The explanation of this has already passed in al-An'am. "An" (that) is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Then, behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾. "Idha" here is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fujā'iyyah, indicating an unexpected occurrence), that is: then, after that, you suddenly became at the time of being human beings spreading over the earth. Although the sudden "idha" most often occurs after the fa', here it occurs after thumma (then), in relation to what befits this particular condition, which is the stages of the human being, as Allah related in several places: from being a sperm-drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone clothed with flesh, he suddenly became humanity. "Intishar" (spreading out) and the meaning of "tantashirun" is: you disperse to what is the sustenance of your livelihoods.

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves﴾, that is: among His signs and indications that point to the resurrection is that He created for you, from your own kind, spouses, that is, of your own species in humanity and mankind. It was said: what is meant is Eve, for He created her from Adam's rib, ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾, that is, you may be familiar with them and incline to them, for two differing kinds do not find tranquility in one another, nor does the heart incline to the other. ﴿And He placed between you affection and mercy﴾, that is: fondness and compassion, through the bond of marriage, by which some of you show kindness to others, without there having been prior acquaintance between you, let alone affection and mercy.

Mujahid said: affection is intercourse, and mercy is offspring; al-Hasan said likewise. al-Suddi said: affection is love, and mercy is tenderness. It was said: affection is a man's love for his wife, and mercy is his compassion toward her, lest any harm befall her.

His saying "that He created for you" is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ mentioned previously, ﴿great in importance, wondrous in clarity, clearly indicating His power, glorified is He, over the resurrection and the raising up, for a people who reflect﴾, because they are the ones who are capable (p-1131) of deducing, since reflection is the material from which it is obtained. As for those heedless of reflection, they are nothing but like cattle.

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, for whoever created these vast bodies, which are the bodies of the heavens and the earth, and made them endure as long as this abode lasts, and created in them wonders of craftsmanship and marvels of formation that are a lesson for those who take heed, is capable of creating you after your death and raising you from your graves. ﴿And the difference of your tongues﴾, that is, your languages, among Arabs and non-Arabs, Turks, Romans and other languages, ﴿and your colors﴾, of whiteness, blackness, redness, yellowness, blueness and greenness, despite your being children of one man and one mother, and despite being gathered under one species, which is humanity, and one differentia, which is rationality, until you became distinguished from one another, so that this is not confused with that, but in every individual among you there is something that distinguishes him from the other individuals. In this is a wondrous power that none understands except those who know, and none comprehends except the reflective. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who know﴾, who are of the kind of this world, without distinction between the righteous and the wicked.

The majority recited the lam of "al-'alamin" with a fatha. Hafs alone recited it with a kasra. al-Farra' said: it has a good justification, for He has said: ﴿signs for a people who understand﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], ﴿signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190], ﴿and none understands them except those who know﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

﴿And among His signs is your sleeping by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty﴾. It was said: there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: and among His signs is your sleeping by night and your seeking of His bounty by day.

It was said: the meaning is sound without inversion, that is: and among His great signs is that you sleep by night and you sleep by day at some times for rest, like the time of qaylula (the afternoon rest), and your seeking of His bounty in both of them, for each of these contains that, though seeking bounty in the day is more frequent.

The first is what is appropriate to the other verses that occur with this meaning, and the second is what is appropriate to the Qur'anic arrangement here.

The reason for mentioning sleep and seeking here, and making them among the proofs of the resurrection, is that sleep resembles death, and the disposing of needs and striving for gains resembles life after death. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾, that is, who hear the signs and admonitions with the hearing of one who reflects and ponders, and so they deduce from that the resurrection.

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope﴾. The meaning: that He shows you. The "an" has been deleted because the context indicates it, as Tarafa said:

"Unquestionably, O you who blame me, let me attend the battles,
and let me witness pleasures; will you make me immortal?"

The sense is: an ahdura (that I attend), and when the particle is deleted in the verse and in the verse of poetry, its governing function is nullified. From this is the well-known proverb: "Hearing of al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him."

It was said: it is by inversion, that is: and He shows you the lightning from among His signs, so it is a conjunction of a verbal sentence to a nominal sentence. It is permissible that "yurikum" is an adjective to a deleted noun, that is: and among His signs is a sign by which and in which He shows you the lightning. It was said: the sense is: and among His signs He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope, from among His signs.

al-Zajjaj said: then it is the conjunction of a sentence to a sentence.

Qatadah said: "Fear for the traveller and hope for the resident." Al-Dahhak said: "Fear of thunderbolts and hope for the rain." Yahya ibn Salam said: "Fear of the hail destroying the crops, and hope for the rain to revive the crops." Ibn Bahr said: "Fear that the lightning will be dry lightning (barq khullub, lightning without rain), and hope that it will bring rain." He recited:

*Let not your lightning be dry lightning,*
*For the best lightning is that which comes with rain.*

The accusatives *khawfan* (fearing) and *tama'an* (hoping) are in the sense of purpose (*'illah*, the grammatical "cause" or reason construction). ﴿And He sends down water from the sky, and with it revives the earth after its death﴾, meaning He revives it with vegetation after it has dried up. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾, for whoever has a share of intellect knows that this is a sign by which the overpowering power is proven.

﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾, meaning their standing and their remaining firm is by His will, glory be to Him, and His power, without any pillar supporting them and without any place on which they rest.

Al-Farra' said: "It means that they endure standing by His command." ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾, meaning: then, after your death and your being placed in the graves, when He calls you with one call, you will come out from them immediately, without delay or hesitation, just as an obedient one responds to the call of an obeyed caller.

*Min al-ard* (from the earth) is connected to *da'a* (called), meaning He calls you from the earth in which you are, as one says, "I called him from the bottom of the valley and he came up to me." Or it is connected to an omitted word that describes *da'wah* (call). Or it is connected to an omitted word indicated by *takhrujun* (you come out), meaning: you came out from the earth. It is not permissible for it to be connected to *takhrujun*, because what follows *idha* (when) does not govern what precedes it. This call is the last blast of Israfil on the Trumpet, as its explanation has already passed. The reciters have agreed on the fatha on the *ta'* in *takhrujun* here. Whoever said it was read here with a damma, in the passive form, was mistaken; it is read with a damma only in *al-A'raf*.

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, from all created beings, in ownership, disposal and creation; none other has any share in that. ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning obedient in submission. It was also said: acknowledging servitude. It was said: praying. It was said: standing on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6], meaning for reckoning. It was said: bearing witness that they are His servants. It was said: sincere.

﴿And it is He who begins creation, then repeats it﴾ after death, so He gives them life, an everlasting life. ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾, meaning easy for Him, He does not find it difficult. Or: "easier for Him" in comparison with your power and with what some of you say to others. Otherwise, nothing in His power is easier than another thing; rather, all things are equal to Him, and He brings them into being by His word: *kun* (be), and it is.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "Whoever takes *ahwan* (easier) as an expression of preferring one thing over another, his view is rejected by His saying ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 169] and by His saying ﴿and their preserving them does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]." The Arabs often use the form *af'al* in the sense of *fa'il*, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*Indeed He who raised the sky built for us*
*A house whose pillars are mighty and tall.*

That is, *'azizah* (mighty) and *tawilah* (tall). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab cited this as evidence:

*Men wished that I would die, and if I die,*
*That is a path in which I am not the only one.*

That is, *lastu bi-wahid* (I am not one alone). Similar is the saying of another:

*By your life, indeed al-Zibriqan is generous*
*With his kindness in hard years, and more excellent.*

That is, *wa-fadil* (and excellent). Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read *wa-huwa 'alayhi hayyin* (and it is easy for Him). Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the repetition is easier for Him than the beginning, that is, more facile, even though all of it is easy.

It was also said: the meaning is that re-creation among created beings is easier than the beginning. It was also said: the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to the created beings, meaning it is easier for the creatures, because they will be called with one cry and they will stand up, and it will be said to them "Be!" and they will be. That is easier for them than becoming a drop of semen, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, through to the end of the stages of creation.

﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾. Al-Khalil said: *al-mathal* means the attribute, that is, His is the highest attribute in the heavens and the earth, as He said ﴿the likeness of Paradise which the righteous have been promised﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 35; Muhammad: 15], meaning its description. Mujahid said: the highest likeness is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and Qatadah said the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning His saying ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾, which He has set forth as an example for you concerning what is difficult and what is easy.

It was also said: the highest likeness is that there is nothing like Him. It was said: it is that whatever He wills comes to be by the word *kun* (be). *Fi al-samawati wal-ard* (in the heavens and the earth) is connected to the meaning of the preceding sentence. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, is known by the highest likeness and described by it in the heavens and the earth. It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word, as a circumstantial description (*hal*) of "the highest", or of "likeness", or of the pronoun in "the highest". He is the Mighty in His dominion, the Overpowering who cannot be overcome, the Wise in His sayings and His deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yublisu* (despair): he said, "it means he becomes miserable." Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported concerning *yublisu*: "he is grieved." And from him: *al-iblas* means disgrace.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yuhbarun* (they will be delighted): he said, "they will be honoured." Al-Daylami reported from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will say: 'Where are those who used to keep their ears and eyes free from the flutes of Satan? Distinguish them.' They will be distinguished by heaps of musk and ambergris. Then He will say to the angels: 'Make them hear My glorification, My praise and My declaration of His oneness.' They will glorify Him with voices the like of which the hearers have never heard before."

Al-Dinawari in *al-Mujalasah* reported from Mujahid, who said: "A caller will call on the Day of Resurrection," and he mentioned something similar, but he did not name the one who narrated it to him from the Messenger of Allah.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Malahi* and al-Isbahani in *al-Targhib* reported something similar from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi, both in *Sifat al-Jannah*, reported, as al-Suyuti said, with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree on a trunk, such that a determined rider would take a hundred years to travel in its shade. The people of Paradise, including the people of the high chambers and others, will come out and converse in its shade. Some of them will long for and mention the amusements of the world, so Allah will send a wind from Paradise which will move that tree with every amusement that existed in the world."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* reported something similar from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Every glorification (*tasbih*) in the Qur'an is prayer (*salah*)." 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Abu Razin, who said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." Then he recited ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾, the prayer of Maghrib, ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾, the prayer of Subh, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾, the prayer of 'Asr, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾, the prayer of Zuhr. And he recited ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [an-Nur: 58].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: "This verse has gathered the times of prayer: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ is Maghrib and 'Isha', ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ is Fajr, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is 'Asr, and ﴿when you enter the noon﴾ is Zuhr."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wal-Layla*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Da'awat* reported from Mu'adh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled [his covenant]? Because he used to say each time he entered the morning and the evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says, when he enters the morning: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾, and ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and revives the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾, he will attain what he missed on that day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening will attain what he missed in that night." Its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾: he said, "obedient," meaning in life, resurrection and death; and they are disobedient to Him in other matters of worship.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "easier (*aysar*)."

Ibn al-Anbari reported from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "The repetition is easier for the created being, because He says to it on the Day of Resurrection, 'Be!' and it is. He began the creation from a drop of semen, then from a clot, then from a lump of flesh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: he said, "There is nothing like Him."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verses 11–27 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Allah originates the creation, then He repeats it﴾. That is, He creates them first, then He restores them after death, living as they were, then to Him you will be returned, to the place of reckoning, where He will recompense the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. He used the singular pronoun in "He repeats it" in consideration of the wording "the creation," and the plural in "you will be returned" in consideration of its meaning.

Abu Bakr and Abu 'Amr recited "yurja'un" (they will be returned) with the yā' (third person).

The rest recited it with the tā' (second person), as an address and a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person) that indicates emphasis.

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will be despairing﴾. The majority of reciters read "yublisu" with the active voice.

al-Sulami recited it in the passive voice. It is said: "Ablasa al-rajul" (the man became despairing) when he fell silent and his argument was cut off.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the mublis (despairing one) is the one who is silent, whose argument is cut off, who has despaired of finding the way to it. From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"O companion, do you recognize a faded, worn-out trace?
He said: 'Yes, I recognize it, and I have been reduced to silence.'"

al-Kalbi said: that is, the polytheists will despair of every good when they witness the punishment. We have already explained the meaning of ibsal (despair) at His saying: ﴿then, behold, they are in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

﴿And they will have no intercessors from among their partners﴾. That is, on the day the Hour is established, the polytheists will have no intercessors from among their partners whom they worshipped besides Allah, to protect them from the punishment of Allah. "And they will be disbelievers in their partners" means, with their idols which they made partners of Allah, they will reject that they are gods, because at that time they will know that they neither benefit nor harm. It was said: the meaning of the verse is that they were disbelievers in the world because of their worship. The first is preferable.

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day they will be separated﴾. That is, all of creation implied by His saying "Allah originates the creation" will be separated, and what is meant by the separation is that each group will be set apart: the believers will go to Paradise, and the disbelievers to the Fire. It does not mean that each individual will be separated from the other. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: (p-1130) ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. This will be after the completion of the reckoning, so they will never be united again.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the manner of their separation, saying: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾. al-Nahhas said: I heard al-Zajjaj say that the meaning of "amma" (as for) is: leave what we were in and take up something else. Likewise Sibawayh said: its meaning is: whatever there may be, then take up other than what we were in. The rawdah (meadow) is every land having plants.

The commentators said: what is meant here is Paradise. The meaning of yuhbarun is they will be made glad. Al-hubur and al-habra are joy. That is: they will be in the gardens of Paradise, enjoying blessings.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the rawdah is what is in a low place; if it is elevated, it is a talah (a raised ground).

Others said: a rawdah is at its best when it is in an elevated place. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Not a meadow from the meadows of al-Hazn, lush with grass,
green, upon which a pouring, abundant rain has fallen."

It was said: the meaning of yuhbarun is they will be honored.

al-Nahhas said: al-Kisa'i related: habartuhu, that is, I honored him and gave him blessings. The preferable interpretation of yuhbarun is "made glad," as is its Arabic meaning, and the very entry into Paradise entails honor and blessing, while gladness is an addition to that.

It was said: al-tahbir is beautification, so the meaning of yuhbarun is that goodness will be done to them. It was said: it is the music that they will hear in Paradise. It was said: other than that. The correct meaning is what we have mentioned.

﴿As for those who disbelieved in Allah and denied Our signs and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, that is, the resurrection, Paradise and the Fire. The indication in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they will be presented in the punishment﴾, that is, they will remain in it. It was said: they will be gathered; it was said: they will descend; it was said: they will be punished. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the perpetuity of their punishment.

Then, when He had explained the end of the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, He guided the believers to that which contains abundant reward and general good.

He said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. The fa' (so) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, that is: when you know that, then glorify Allah, that is, declare Him free of what is unfitting for Him, in the time of morning and evening, and in the afternoon and at midday.

It was said: what is meant by tasbih here is the five daily prayers. So His saying "when you enter the evening" is the prayers of maghrib and 'isha', His saying "and when you enter the morning" is the prayer of fajr, His saying "and in the afternoon" is the prayer of 'asr, and His saying "when you reach midday" is the prayer of zuhr. Thus said al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others.

al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: the meaning of "so glorify Allah" is "so pray to Allah."

al-Nahhas said: the people of tafsir hold that this verse concerns the prayers. He said: I heard Muhammad ibn Zayd say: its reality, in my view, is "so glorify Allah in the prayers," because glorification occurs in prayer. The clause ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'tarida, interjected between parts of a sentence), brought to guide to praise and to indicate the legitimacy of combining it with glorification, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾ [al-Hijr: 98] and His saying: ﴿while we glorify with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. It was said: the meaning of "and to Him belongs praise" is the exclusivity to Him of the prayer in which praise is recited. The first is preferable.

Ikrimah recited "hinan tumsuna wa hinan tusbihuna" (at a time when you enter the evening and at a time when you enter the morning). The meaning is: at a time when you enter the evening in it and at a time when you enter the morning in it. "Al-'ashiyy" (the evening) runs from the maghrib prayer to the 'atamah (the late night). Al-Jawhari said this. Others said: it runs from the decline of the sun to the rising of dawn. From this is the saying of the poet:

"We set out at dawn, in the pre-dawn darkness of the night,
and in the evening, after the middle of the day had passed."

His saying "'ashiyyan" (in the afternoon) is conjoined to "hina" (at a time). "In the heavens and the earth" is connected to the praise itself, that is: the praise to Him takes place in the heavens and the earth.

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, like the human from the sperm-drop, and the bird from the egg; ﴿and He brings the dead out of the living﴾, like the sperm-drop and the egg from the animal.

The explanation of this has already passed in the surah of Al 'Imran.

It was said: the connection of this verse with the preceding one is that a person, at morning, emerges from a semblance of death, which is sleep, into a semblance of existence, which is wakefulness; and at night he emerges from wakefulness into sleep. ﴿And He revives the earth after its death﴾, that is, He revives it with plants after its death by dryness. This is similar to bringing the living out of the dead. ﴿And thus you will be brought out﴾, that is, like that bringing out you will be brought out of your graves.

The majority recited "tukhrajun" (you will be brought out) in the passive voice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it in the active voice, attributing the going out to them, as in His saying: ﴿On the day they come forth from the graves﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43].

﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, that is, among His dazzling signs that indicate the resurrection is that He created you, that is, created your father Adam from dust, and created you within His creation of him, because the branch is drawn from the root and taken from it. The explanation of this has already passed in al-An'am. "An" (that) is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Then, behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾. "Idha" here is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fujā'iyyah, indicating an unexpected occurrence), that is: then, after that, you suddenly became at the time of being human beings spreading over the earth. Although the sudden "idha" most often occurs after the fa', here it occurs after thumma (then), in relation to what befits this particular condition, which is the stages of the human being, as Allah related in several places: from being a sperm-drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone clothed with flesh, he suddenly became humanity. "Intishar" (spreading out) and the meaning of "tantashirun" is: you disperse to what is the sustenance of your livelihoods.

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves﴾, that is: among His signs and indications that point to the resurrection is that He created for you, from your own kind, spouses, that is, of your own species in humanity and mankind. It was said: what is meant is Eve, for He created her from Adam's rib, ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾, that is, you may be familiar with them and incline to them, for two differing kinds do not find tranquility in one another, nor does the heart incline to the other. ﴿And He placed between you affection and mercy﴾, that is: fondness and compassion, through the bond of marriage, by which some of you show kindness to others, without there having been prior acquaintance between you, let alone affection and mercy.

Mujahid said: affection is intercourse, and mercy is offspring; al-Hasan said likewise. al-Suddi said: affection is love, and mercy is tenderness. It was said: affection is a man's love for his wife, and mercy is his compassion toward her, lest any harm befall her.

His saying "that He created for you" is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ mentioned previously, ﴿great in importance, wondrous in clarity, clearly indicating His power, glorified is He, over the resurrection and the raising up, for a people who reflect﴾, because they are the ones who are capable (p-1131) of deducing, since reflection is the material from which it is obtained. As for those heedless of reflection, they are nothing but like cattle.

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, for whoever created these vast bodies, which are the bodies of the heavens and the earth, and made them endure as long as this abode lasts, and created in them wonders of craftsmanship and marvels of formation that are a lesson for those who take heed, is capable of creating you after your death and raising you from your graves. ﴿And the difference of your tongues﴾, that is, your languages, among Arabs and non-Arabs, Turks, Romans and other languages, ﴿and your colors﴾, of whiteness, blackness, redness, yellowness, blueness and greenness, despite your being children of one man and one mother, and despite being gathered under one species, which is humanity, and one differentia, which is rationality, until you became distinguished from one another, so that this is not confused with that, but in every individual among you there is something that distinguishes him from the other individuals. In this is a wondrous power that none understands except those who know, and none comprehends except the reflective. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who know﴾, who are of the kind of this world, without distinction between the righteous and the wicked.

The majority recited the lam of "al-'alamin" with a fatha. Hafs alone recited it with a kasra. al-Farra' said: it has a good justification, for He has said: ﴿signs for a people who understand﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], ﴿signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190], ﴿and none understands them except those who know﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

﴿And among His signs is your sleeping by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty﴾. It was said: there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: and among His signs is your sleeping by night and your seeking of His bounty by day.

It was said: the meaning is sound without inversion, that is: and among His great signs is that you sleep by night and you sleep by day at some times for rest, like the time of qaylula (the afternoon rest), and your seeking of His bounty in both of them, for each of these contains that, though seeking bounty in the day is more frequent.

The first is what is appropriate to the other verses that occur with this meaning, and the second is what is appropriate to the Qur'anic arrangement here.

The reason for mentioning sleep and seeking here, and making them among the proofs of the resurrection, is that sleep resembles death, and the disposing of needs and striving for gains resembles life after death. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾, that is, who hear the signs and admonitions with the hearing of one who reflects and ponders, and so they deduce from that the resurrection.

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope﴾. The meaning: that He shows you. The "an" has been deleted because the context indicates it, as Tarafa said:

"Unquestionably, O you who blame me, let me attend the battles,
and let me witness pleasures; will you make me immortal?"

The sense is: an ahdura (that I attend), and when the particle is deleted in the verse and in the verse of poetry, its governing function is nullified. From this is the well-known proverb: "Hearing of al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him."

It was said: it is by inversion, that is: and He shows you the lightning from among His signs, so it is a conjunction of a verbal sentence to a nominal sentence. It is permissible that "yurikum" is an adjective to a deleted noun, that is: and among His signs is a sign by which and in which He shows you the lightning. It was said: the sense is: and among His signs He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope, from among His signs.

al-Zajjaj said: then it is the conjunction of a sentence to a sentence.

Qatadah said: "Fear for the traveller and hope for the resident." Al-Dahhak said: "Fear of thunderbolts and hope for the rain." Yahya ibn Salam said: "Fear of the hail destroying the crops, and hope for the rain to revive the crops." Ibn Bahr said: "Fear that the lightning will be dry lightning (barq khullub, lightning without rain), and hope that it will bring rain." He recited:

*Let not your lightning be dry lightning,*
*For the best lightning is that which comes with rain.*

The accusatives *khawfan* (fearing) and *tama'an* (hoping) are in the sense of purpose (*'illah*, the grammatical "cause" or reason construction). ﴿And He sends down water from the sky, and with it revives the earth after its death﴾, meaning He revives it with vegetation after it has dried up. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾, for whoever has a share of intellect knows that this is a sign by which the overpowering power is proven.

﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾, meaning their standing and their remaining firm is by His will, glory be to Him, and His power, without any pillar supporting them and without any place on which they rest.

Al-Farra' said: "It means that they endure standing by His command." ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾, meaning: then, after your death and your being placed in the graves, when He calls you with one call, you will come out from them immediately, without delay or hesitation, just as an obedient one responds to the call of an obeyed caller.

*Min al-ard* (from the earth) is connected to *da'a* (called), meaning He calls you from the earth in which you are, as one says, "I called him from the bottom of the valley and he came up to me." Or it is connected to an omitted word that describes *da'wah* (call). Or it is connected to an omitted word indicated by *takhrujun* (you come out), meaning: you came out from the earth. It is not permissible for it to be connected to *takhrujun*, because what follows *idha* (when) does not govern what precedes it. This call is the last blast of Israfil on the Trumpet, as its explanation has already passed. The reciters have agreed on the fatha on the *ta'* in *takhrujun* here. Whoever said it was read here with a damma, in the passive form, was mistaken; it is read with a damma only in *al-A'raf*.

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, from all created beings, in ownership, disposal and creation; none other has any share in that. ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning obedient in submission. It was also said: acknowledging servitude. It was said: praying. It was said: standing on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6], meaning for reckoning. It was said: bearing witness that they are His servants. It was said: sincere.

﴿And it is He who begins creation, then repeats it﴾ after death, so He gives them life, an everlasting life. ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾, meaning easy for Him, He does not find it difficult. Or: "easier for Him" in comparison with your power and with what some of you say to others. Otherwise, nothing in His power is easier than another thing; rather, all things are equal to Him, and He brings them into being by His word: *kun* (be), and it is.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "Whoever takes *ahwan* (easier) as an expression of preferring one thing over another, his view is rejected by His saying ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 169] and by His saying ﴿and their preserving them does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]." The Arabs often use the form *af'al* in the sense of *fa'il*, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*Indeed He who raised the sky built for us*
*A house whose pillars are mighty and tall.*

That is, *'azizah* (mighty) and *tawilah* (tall). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab cited this as evidence:

*Men wished that I would die, and if I die,*
*That is a path in which I am not the only one.*

That is, *lastu bi-wahid* (I am not one alone). Similar is the saying of another:

*By your life, indeed al-Zibriqan is generous*
*With his kindness in hard years, and more excellent.*

That is, *wa-fadil* (and excellent). Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read *wa-huwa 'alayhi hayyin* (and it is easy for Him). Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the repetition is easier for Him than the beginning, that is, more facile, even though all of it is easy.

It was also said: the meaning is that re-creation among created beings is easier than the beginning. It was also said: the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to the created beings, meaning it is easier for the creatures, because they will be called with one cry and they will stand up, and it will be said to them "Be!" and they will be. That is easier for them than becoming a drop of semen, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, through to the end of the stages of creation.

﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾. Al-Khalil said: *al-mathal* means the attribute, that is, His is the highest attribute in the heavens and the earth, as He said ﴿the likeness of Paradise which the righteous have been promised﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 35; Muhammad: 15], meaning its description. Mujahid said: the highest likeness is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and Qatadah said the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning His saying ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾, which He has set forth as an example for you concerning what is difficult and what is easy.

It was also said: the highest likeness is that there is nothing like Him. It was said: it is that whatever He wills comes to be by the word *kun* (be). *Fi al-samawati wal-ard* (in the heavens and the earth) is connected to the meaning of the preceding sentence. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, is known by the highest likeness and described by it in the heavens and the earth. It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word, as a circumstantial description (*hal*) of "the highest", or of "likeness", or of the pronoun in "the highest". He is the Mighty in His dominion, the Overpowering who cannot be overcome, the Wise in His sayings and His deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yublisu* (despair): he said, "it means he becomes miserable." Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported concerning *yublisu*: "he is grieved." And from him: *al-iblas* means disgrace.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yuhbarun* (they will be delighted): he said, "they will be honoured." Al-Daylami reported from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will say: 'Where are those who used to keep their ears and eyes free from the flutes of Satan? Distinguish them.' They will be distinguished by heaps of musk and ambergris. Then He will say to the angels: 'Make them hear My glorification, My praise and My declaration of His oneness.' They will glorify Him with voices the like of which the hearers have never heard before."

Al-Dinawari in *al-Mujalasah* reported from Mujahid, who said: "A caller will call on the Day of Resurrection," and he mentioned something similar, but he did not name the one who narrated it to him from the Messenger of Allah.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Malahi* and al-Isbahani in *al-Targhib* reported something similar from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi, both in *Sifat al-Jannah*, reported, as al-Suyuti said, with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree on a trunk, such that a determined rider would take a hundred years to travel in its shade. The people of Paradise, including the people of the high chambers and others, will come out and converse in its shade. Some of them will long for and mention the amusements of the world, so Allah will send a wind from Paradise which will move that tree with every amusement that existed in the world."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* reported something similar from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Every glorification (*tasbih*) in the Qur'an is prayer (*salah*)." 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Abu Razin, who said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." Then he recited ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾, the prayer of Maghrib, ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾, the prayer of Subh, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾, the prayer of 'Asr, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾, the prayer of Zuhr. And he recited ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [an-Nur: 58].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: "This verse has gathered the times of prayer: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ is Maghrib and 'Isha', ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ is Fajr, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is 'Asr, and ﴿when you enter the noon﴾ is Zuhr."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wal-Layla*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Da'awat* reported from Mu'adh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled [his covenant]? Because he used to say each time he entered the morning and the evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says, when he enters the morning: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾, and ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and revives the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾, he will attain what he missed on that day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening will attain what he missed in that night." Its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾: he said, "obedient," meaning in life, resurrection and death; and they are disobedient to Him in other matters of worship.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "easier (*aysar*)."

Ibn al-Anbari reported from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "The repetition is easier for the created being, because He says to it on the Day of Resurrection, 'Be!' and it is. He began the creation from a drop of semen, then from a clot, then from a lump of flesh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: he said, "There is nothing like Him."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verses 11–27 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Allah originates the creation, then He repeats it﴾. That is, He creates them first, then He restores them after death, living as they were, then to Him you will be returned, to the place of reckoning, where He will recompense the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. He used the singular pronoun in "He repeats it" in consideration of the wording "the creation," and the plural in "you will be returned" in consideration of its meaning.

Abu Bakr and Abu 'Amr recited "yurja'un" (they will be returned) with the yā' (third person).

The rest recited it with the tā' (second person), as an address and a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person) that indicates emphasis.

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will be despairing﴾. The majority of reciters read "yublisu" with the active voice.

al-Sulami recited it in the passive voice. It is said: "Ablasa al-rajul" (the man became despairing) when he fell silent and his argument was cut off.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the mublis (despairing one) is the one who is silent, whose argument is cut off, who has despaired of finding the way to it. From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"O companion, do you recognize a faded, worn-out trace?
He said: 'Yes, I recognize it, and I have been reduced to silence.'"

al-Kalbi said: that is, the polytheists will despair of every good when they witness the punishment. We have already explained the meaning of ibsal (despair) at His saying: ﴿then, behold, they are in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

﴿And they will have no intercessors from among their partners﴾. That is, on the day the Hour is established, the polytheists will have no intercessors from among their partners whom they worshipped besides Allah, to protect them from the punishment of Allah. "And they will be disbelievers in their partners" means, with their idols which they made partners of Allah, they will reject that they are gods, because at that time they will know that they neither benefit nor harm. It was said: the meaning of the verse is that they were disbelievers in the world because of their worship. The first is preferable.

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day they will be separated﴾. That is, all of creation implied by His saying "Allah originates the creation" will be separated, and what is meant by the separation is that each group will be set apart: the believers will go to Paradise, and the disbelievers to the Fire. It does not mean that each individual will be separated from the other. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: (p-1130) ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. This will be after the completion of the reckoning, so they will never be united again.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the manner of their separation, saying: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾. al-Nahhas said: I heard al-Zajjaj say that the meaning of "amma" (as for) is: leave what we were in and take up something else. Likewise Sibawayh said: its meaning is: whatever there may be, then take up other than what we were in. The rawdah (meadow) is every land having plants.

The commentators said: what is meant here is Paradise. The meaning of yuhbarun is they will be made glad. Al-hubur and al-habra are joy. That is: they will be in the gardens of Paradise, enjoying blessings.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the rawdah is what is in a low place; if it is elevated, it is a talah (a raised ground).

Others said: a rawdah is at its best when it is in an elevated place. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Not a meadow from the meadows of al-Hazn, lush with grass,
green, upon which a pouring, abundant rain has fallen."

It was said: the meaning of yuhbarun is they will be honored.

al-Nahhas said: al-Kisa'i related: habartuhu, that is, I honored him and gave him blessings. The preferable interpretation of yuhbarun is "made glad," as is its Arabic meaning, and the very entry into Paradise entails honor and blessing, while gladness is an addition to that.

It was said: al-tahbir is beautification, so the meaning of yuhbarun is that goodness will be done to them. It was said: it is the music that they will hear in Paradise. It was said: other than that. The correct meaning is what we have mentioned.

﴿As for those who disbelieved in Allah and denied Our signs and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, that is, the resurrection, Paradise and the Fire. The indication in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they will be presented in the punishment﴾, that is, they will remain in it. It was said: they will be gathered; it was said: they will descend; it was said: they will be punished. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the perpetuity of their punishment.

Then, when He had explained the end of the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, He guided the believers to that which contains abundant reward and general good.

He said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. The fa' (so) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, that is: when you know that, then glorify Allah, that is, declare Him free of what is unfitting for Him, in the time of morning and evening, and in the afternoon and at midday.

It was said: what is meant by tasbih here is the five daily prayers. So His saying "when you enter the evening" is the prayers of maghrib and 'isha', His saying "and when you enter the morning" is the prayer of fajr, His saying "and in the afternoon" is the prayer of 'asr, and His saying "when you reach midday" is the prayer of zuhr. Thus said al-Dahhak, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others.

al-Wahidi said: the commentators said: the meaning of "so glorify Allah" is "so pray to Allah."

al-Nahhas said: the people of tafsir hold that this verse concerns the prayers. He said: I heard Muhammad ibn Zayd say: its reality, in my view, is "so glorify Allah in the prayers," because glorification occurs in prayer. The clause ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'tarida, interjected between parts of a sentence), brought to guide to praise and to indicate the legitimacy of combining it with glorification, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾ [al-Hijr: 98] and His saying: ﴿while we glorify with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. It was said: the meaning of "and to Him belongs praise" is the exclusivity to Him of the prayer in which praise is recited. The first is preferable.

Ikrimah recited "hinan tumsuna wa hinan tusbihuna" (at a time when you enter the evening and at a time when you enter the morning). The meaning is: at a time when you enter the evening in it and at a time when you enter the morning in it. "Al-'ashiyy" (the evening) runs from the maghrib prayer to the 'atamah (the late night). Al-Jawhari said this. Others said: it runs from the decline of the sun to the rising of dawn. From this is the saying of the poet:

"We set out at dawn, in the pre-dawn darkness of the night,
and in the evening, after the middle of the day had passed."

His saying "'ashiyyan" (in the afternoon) is conjoined to "hina" (at a time). "In the heavens and the earth" is connected to the praise itself, that is: the praise to Him takes place in the heavens and the earth.

﴿He brings the living out of the dead﴾, like the human from the sperm-drop, and the bird from the egg; ﴿and He brings the dead out of the living﴾, like the sperm-drop and the egg from the animal.

The explanation of this has already passed in the surah of Al 'Imran.

It was said: the connection of this verse with the preceding one is that a person, at morning, emerges from a semblance of death, which is sleep, into a semblance of existence, which is wakefulness; and at night he emerges from wakefulness into sleep. ﴿And He revives the earth after its death﴾, that is, He revives it with plants after its death by dryness. This is similar to bringing the living out of the dead. ﴿And thus you will be brought out﴾, that is, like that bringing out you will be brought out of your graves.

The majority recited "tukhrajun" (you will be brought out) in the passive voice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it in the active voice, attributing the going out to them, as in His saying: ﴿On the day they come forth from the graves﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43].

﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, that is, among His dazzling signs that indicate the resurrection is that He created you, that is, created your father Adam from dust, and created you within His creation of him, because the branch is drawn from the root and taken from it. The explanation of this has already passed in al-An'am. "An" (that) is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Then, behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾. "Idha" here is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fujā'iyyah, indicating an unexpected occurrence), that is: then, after that, you suddenly became at the time of being human beings spreading over the earth. Although the sudden "idha" most often occurs after the fa', here it occurs after thumma (then), in relation to what befits this particular condition, which is the stages of the human being, as Allah related in several places: from being a sperm-drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone clothed with flesh, he suddenly became humanity. "Intishar" (spreading out) and the meaning of "tantashirun" is: you disperse to what is the sustenance of your livelihoods.

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves﴾, that is: among His signs and indications that point to the resurrection is that He created for you, from your own kind, spouses, that is, of your own species in humanity and mankind. It was said: what is meant is Eve, for He created her from Adam's rib, ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾, that is, you may be familiar with them and incline to them, for two differing kinds do not find tranquility in one another, nor does the heart incline to the other. ﴿And He placed between you affection and mercy﴾, that is: fondness and compassion, through the bond of marriage, by which some of you show kindness to others, without there having been prior acquaintance between you, let alone affection and mercy.

Mujahid said: affection is intercourse, and mercy is offspring; al-Hasan said likewise. al-Suddi said: affection is love, and mercy is tenderness. It was said: affection is a man's love for his wife, and mercy is his compassion toward her, lest any harm befall her.

His saying "that He created for you" is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ mentioned previously, ﴿great in importance, wondrous in clarity, clearly indicating His power, glorified is He, over the resurrection and the raising up, for a people who reflect﴾, because they are the ones who are capable (p-1131) of deducing, since reflection is the material from which it is obtained. As for those heedless of reflection, they are nothing but like cattle.

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, for whoever created these vast bodies, which are the bodies of the heavens and the earth, and made them endure as long as this abode lasts, and created in them wonders of craftsmanship and marvels of formation that are a lesson for those who take heed, is capable of creating you after your death and raising you from your graves. ﴿And the difference of your tongues﴾, that is, your languages, among Arabs and non-Arabs, Turks, Romans and other languages, ﴿and your colors﴾, of whiteness, blackness, redness, yellowness, blueness and greenness, despite your being children of one man and one mother, and despite being gathered under one species, which is humanity, and one differentia, which is rationality, until you became distinguished from one another, so that this is not confused with that, but in every individual among you there is something that distinguishes him from the other individuals. In this is a wondrous power that none understands except those who know, and none comprehends except the reflective. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who know﴾, who are of the kind of this world, without distinction between the righteous and the wicked.

The majority recited the lam of "al-'alamin" with a fatha. Hafs alone recited it with a kasra. al-Farra' said: it has a good justification, for He has said: ﴿signs for a people who understand﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], ﴿signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190], ﴿and none understands them except those who know﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

﴿And among His signs is your sleeping by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty﴾. It was said: there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: and among His signs is your sleeping by night and your seeking of His bounty by day.

It was said: the meaning is sound without inversion, that is: and among His great signs is that you sleep by night and you sleep by day at some times for rest, like the time of qaylula (the afternoon rest), and your seeking of His bounty in both of them, for each of these contains that, though seeking bounty in the day is more frequent.

The first is what is appropriate to the other verses that occur with this meaning, and the second is what is appropriate to the Qur'anic arrangement here.

The reason for mentioning sleep and seeking here, and making them among the proofs of the resurrection, is that sleep resembles death, and the disposing of needs and striving for gains resembles life after death. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾, that is, who hear the signs and admonitions with the hearing of one who reflects and ponders, and so they deduce from that the resurrection.

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope﴾. The meaning: that He shows you. The "an" has been deleted because the context indicates it, as Tarafa said:

"Unquestionably, O you who blame me, let me attend the battles,
and let me witness pleasures; will you make me immortal?"

The sense is: an ahdura (that I attend), and when the particle is deleted in the verse and in the verse of poetry, its governing function is nullified. From this is the well-known proverb: "Hearing of al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him."

It was said: it is by inversion, that is: and He shows you the lightning from among His signs, so it is a conjunction of a verbal sentence to a nominal sentence. It is permissible that "yurikum" is an adjective to a deleted noun, that is: and among His signs is a sign by which and in which He shows you the lightning. It was said: the sense is: and among His signs He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope, from among His signs.

al-Zajjaj said: then it is the conjunction of a sentence to a sentence.

Qatadah said: "Fear for the traveller and hope for the resident." Al-Dahhak said: "Fear of thunderbolts and hope for the rain." Yahya ibn Salam said: "Fear of the hail destroying the crops, and hope for the rain to revive the crops." Ibn Bahr said: "Fear that the lightning will be dry lightning (barq khullub, lightning without rain), and hope that it will bring rain." He recited:

*Let not your lightning be dry lightning,*
*For the best lightning is that which comes with rain.*

The accusatives *khawfan* (fearing) and *tama'an* (hoping) are in the sense of purpose (*'illah*, the grammatical "cause" or reason construction). ﴿And He sends down water from the sky, and with it revives the earth after its death﴾, meaning He revives it with vegetation after it has dried up. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾, for whoever has a share of intellect knows that this is a sign by which the overpowering power is proven.

﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾, meaning their standing and their remaining firm is by His will, glory be to Him, and His power, without any pillar supporting them and without any place on which they rest.

Al-Farra' said: "It means that they endure standing by His command." ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾, meaning: then, after your death and your being placed in the graves, when He calls you with one call, you will come out from them immediately, without delay or hesitation, just as an obedient one responds to the call of an obeyed caller.

*Min al-ard* (from the earth) is connected to *da'a* (called), meaning He calls you from the earth in which you are, as one says, "I called him from the bottom of the valley and he came up to me." Or it is connected to an omitted word that describes *da'wah* (call). Or it is connected to an omitted word indicated by *takhrujun* (you come out), meaning: you came out from the earth. It is not permissible for it to be connected to *takhrujun*, because what follows *idha* (when) does not govern what precedes it. This call is the last blast of Israfil on the Trumpet, as its explanation has already passed. The reciters have agreed on the fatha on the *ta'* in *takhrujun* here. Whoever said it was read here with a damma, in the passive form, was mistaken; it is read with a damma only in *al-A'raf*.

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, from all created beings, in ownership, disposal and creation; none other has any share in that. ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning obedient in submission. It was also said: acknowledging servitude. It was said: praying. It was said: standing on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6], meaning for reckoning. It was said: bearing witness that they are His servants. It was said: sincere.

﴿And it is He who begins creation, then repeats it﴾ after death, so He gives them life, an everlasting life. ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾, meaning easy for Him, He does not find it difficult. Or: "easier for Him" in comparison with your power and with what some of you say to others. Otherwise, nothing in His power is easier than another thing; rather, all things are equal to Him, and He brings them into being by His word: *kun* (be), and it is.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "Whoever takes *ahwan* (easier) as an expression of preferring one thing over another, his view is rejected by His saying ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 169] and by His saying ﴿and their preserving them does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]." The Arabs often use the form *af'al* in the sense of *fa'il*, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*Indeed He who raised the sky built for us*
*A house whose pillars are mighty and tall.*

That is, *'azizah* (mighty) and *tawilah* (tall). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab cited this as evidence:

*Men wished that I would die, and if I die,*
*That is a path in which I am not the only one.*

That is, *lastu bi-wahid* (I am not one alone). Similar is the saying of another:

*By your life, indeed al-Zibriqan is generous*
*With his kindness in hard years, and more excellent.*

That is, *wa-fadil* (and excellent). Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read *wa-huwa 'alayhi hayyin* (and it is easy for Him). Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the repetition is easier for Him than the beginning, that is, more facile, even though all of it is easy.

It was also said: the meaning is that re-creation among created beings is easier than the beginning. It was also said: the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to the created beings, meaning it is easier for the creatures, because they will be called with one cry and they will stand up, and it will be said to them "Be!" and they will be. That is easier for them than becoming a drop of semen, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, through to the end of the stages of creation.

﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾. Al-Khalil said: *al-mathal* means the attribute, that is, His is the highest attribute in the heavens and the earth, as He said ﴿the likeness of Paradise which the righteous have been promised﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 35; Muhammad: 15], meaning its description. Mujahid said: the highest likeness is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and Qatadah said the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning His saying ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾, which He has set forth as an example for you concerning what is difficult and what is easy.

It was also said: the highest likeness is that there is nothing like Him. It was said: it is that whatever He wills comes to be by the word *kun* (be). *Fi al-samawati wal-ard* (in the heavens and the earth) is connected to the meaning of the preceding sentence. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, is known by the highest likeness and described by it in the heavens and the earth. It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word, as a circumstantial description (*hal*) of "the highest", or of "likeness", or of the pronoun in "the highest". He is the Mighty in His dominion, the Overpowering who cannot be overcome, the Wise in His sayings and His deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yublisu* (despair): he said, "it means he becomes miserable." Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported concerning *yublisu*: "he is grieved." And from him: *al-iblas* means disgrace.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yuhbarun* (they will be delighted): he said, "they will be honoured." Al-Daylami reported from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will say: 'Where are those who used to keep their ears and eyes free from the flutes of Satan? Distinguish them.' They will be distinguished by heaps of musk and ambergris. Then He will say to the angels: 'Make them hear My glorification, My praise and My declaration of His oneness.' They will glorify Him with voices the like of which the hearers have never heard before."

Al-Dinawari in *al-Mujalasah* reported from Mujahid, who said: "A caller will call on the Day of Resurrection," and he mentioned something similar, but he did not name the one who narrated it to him from the Messenger of Allah.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Malahi* and al-Isbahani in *al-Targhib* reported something similar from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi, both in *Sifat al-Jannah*, reported, as al-Suyuti said, with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree on a trunk, such that a determined rider would take a hundred years to travel in its shade. The people of Paradise, including the people of the high chambers and others, will come out and converse in its shade. Some of them will long for and mention the amusements of the world, so Allah will send a wind from Paradise which will move that tree with every amusement that existed in the world."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* reported something similar from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Every glorification (*tasbih*) in the Qur'an is prayer (*salah*)." 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Abu Razin, who said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." Then he recited ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾, the prayer of Maghrib, ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾, the prayer of Subh, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾, the prayer of 'Asr, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾, the prayer of Zuhr. And he recited ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [an-Nur: 58].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: "This verse has gathered the times of prayer: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ is Maghrib and 'Isha', ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ is Fajr, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is 'Asr, and ﴿when you enter the noon﴾ is Zuhr."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wal-Layla*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Da'awat* reported from Mu'adh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled [his covenant]? Because he used to say each time he entered the morning and the evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says, when he enters the morning: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾, and ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and revives the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾, he will attain what he missed on that day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening will attain what he missed in that night." Its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾: he said, "obedient," meaning in life, resurrection and death; and they are disobedient to Him in other matters of worship.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "easier (*aysar*)."

Ibn al-Anbari reported from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "The repetition is easier for the created being, because He says to it on the Day of Resurrection, 'Be!' and it is. He began the creation from a drop of semen, then from a clot, then from a lump of flesh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: he said, "There is nothing like Him."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verses 11–27 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Allah originates the creation, then He repeats it﴾. That is, He creates them first, then He restores them after death, living as they were, then to Him you will be returned, to the place of reckoning, where He will recompense the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil. He used the singular pronoun in "He repeats it" in consideration of the wording "the creation," and the plural in "you will be returned" in consideration of its meaning.

Abu Bakr and Abu 'Amr recited "yurja'un" (they will be returned) with the yā' (third person).

The rest recited it with the tā' (second person), as an address and a shift (iltifat, a change of grammatical person) that indicates emphasis.

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will be despairing﴾. The majority of reciters read "yublisu" with the active voice.

al-Sulami recited it in the passive voice. It is said: "Ablasa al-rajul" (the man became despairing) when he fell silent and his argument was cut off.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the mublis (despairing one) is the one who is silent, whose argument is cut off, who has despaired of finding the way to it. From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"O companion, do you recognize a faded, worn-out trace?
He said: 'Yes, I recognize it, and I have been reduced to silence.'"

al-Kalbi said: that is, the polytheists will despair of every good when they witness the punishment. We have already explained the meaning of ibsal (despair) at His saying: ﴿then, behold, they are in despair﴾ [al-An'am: 44].

﴿And they will have no intercessors from among their partners﴾. That is, on the day the Hour is established, the polytheists will have no intercessors from among their partners whom they worshipped besides Allah, to protect them from the punishment of Allah. "And they will be disbelievers in their partners" means, with their idols which they made partners of Allah, they will reject that they are gods, because at that time they will know that they neither benefit nor harm. It was said: the meaning of the verse is that they were disbelievers in the world because of their worship. The first is preferable.

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, on that day they will be separated﴾. That is, all of creation implied by His saying "Allah originates the creation" will be separated, and what is meant by the separation is that each group will be set apart: the believers will go to Paradise, and the disbelievers to the Fire. It does not mean that each individual will be separated from the other. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: (p-1130) ﴿A party in Paradise and a party in the Blaze﴾ [al-Shura: 7]. This will be after the completion of the reckoning, so they will never be united again.

Then He, glorified is He, explained the manner of their separation, saying: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾. al-Nahhas said: I heard al-Zajjaj say that the meaning of "amma" (as for) is: leave what we were in and take up something else. Likewise Sibawayh said: its meaning is: whatever there may be, then take up other than what we were in. The rawdah (meadow) is every land having plants.

The commentators said: what is meant here is Paradise. The meaning of yuhbarun is they will be made glad. Al-hubur and al-habra are joy. That is: they will be in the gardens of Paradise, enjoying blessings.

Abu 'Ubayd said: the rawdah is what is in a low place; if it is elevated, it is a talah (a raised ground).

Others said: a rawdah is at its best when it is in an elevated place. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Not a meadow from the meadows of al-Hazn, lush with grass,
green, upon which a pouring, abundant rain has fallen."

It was said: the meaning of yuhbarun is they will be honored.

al-Nahhas said: al-Kisa'i related: habartuhu, that is, I honored him and gave him blessings. The preferable interpretation of yuhbarun is "made glad," as is its Arabic meaning, and the very entry into Paradise entails honor and blessing, while gladness is an addition to that.

It was said: al-tahbir is beautification, so the meaning of yuhbarun is that goodness will be done to them. It was said: it is the music that they will hear in Paradise. It was said: other than that. The correct meaning is what we have mentioned.

﴿As for those who disbelieved in Allah and denied Our signs and denied the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, that is, the resurrection, Paradise and the Fire. The indication in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. It is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they will be presented in the punishment﴾, that is, they will remain in it. It was said: they will be gathered; it was said: they will descend; it was said: they will be punished. The meanings are close, and what is meant is the perpetuity of their punishment.

Then, when He had explained the end of the group of believers and the group of disbelievers, He guided the believers to that which contains abundant reward and general good.

He said: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾. The fa' (so) indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes it, that is: when you know that, then glorify Allah, that is, declare Him free of what is unfitting for Him, in the time of morning and evening, and in the afternoon and at midday.

It was said: what is meant by tasbih here is the five daily prayers.
