It was said: the connection of this verse with the preceding one is that a person, at morning, emerges from a semblance of death, which is sleep, into a semblance of existence, which is wakefulness; and at night he emerges from wakefulness into sleep. ﴿And He revives the earth after its death﴾, that is, He revives it with plants after its death by dryness. This is similar to bringing the living out of the dead. ﴿And thus you will be brought out﴾, that is, like that bringing out you will be brought out of your graves.

The majority recited "tukhrajun" (you will be brought out) in the passive voice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it in the active voice, attributing the going out to them, as in His saying: ﴿On the day they come forth from the graves﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43].

﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, that is, among His dazzling signs that indicate the resurrection is that He created you, that is, created your father Adam from dust, and created you within His creation of him, because the branch is drawn from the root and taken from it. The explanation of this has already passed in al-An'am. "An" (that) is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Then, behold, you are human beings spreading out﴾. "Idha" here is the sudden "idha" (idha al-fujā'iyyah, indicating an unexpected occurrence), that is: then, after that, you suddenly became at the time of being human beings spreading over the earth. Although the sudden "idha" most often occurs after the fa', here it occurs after thumma (then), in relation to what befits this particular condition, which is the stages of the human being, as Allah related in several places: from being a sperm-drop, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, then bone clothed with flesh, he suddenly became humanity. "Intishar" (spreading out) and the meaning of "tantashirun" is: you disperse to what is the sustenance of your livelihoods.

﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from yourselves﴾, that is: among His signs and indications that point to the resurrection is that He created for you, from your own kind, spouses, that is, of your own species in humanity and mankind. It was said: what is meant is Eve, for He created her from Adam's rib, ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾, that is, you may be familiar with them and incline to them, for two differing kinds do not find tranquility in one another, nor does the heart incline to the other. ﴿And He placed between you affection and mercy﴾, that is: fondness and compassion, through the bond of marriage, by which some of you show kindness to others, without there having been prior acquaintance between you, let alone affection and mercy.

Mujahid said: affection is intercourse, and mercy is offspring; al-Hasan said likewise. al-Suddi said: affection is love, and mercy is tenderness. It was said: affection is a man's love for his wife, and mercy is his compassion toward her, lest any harm befall her.

His saying "that He created for you" is in the position of a nominative by beginning, and "from among His signs" is its predicate. ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾ mentioned previously, ﴿great in importance, wondrous in clarity, clearly indicating His power, glorified is He, over the resurrection and the raising up, for a people who reflect﴾, because they are the ones who are capable (p-1131) of deducing, since reflection is the material from which it is obtained. As for those heedless of reflection, they are nothing but like cattle.

﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, for whoever created these vast bodies, which are the bodies of the heavens and the earth, and made them endure as long as this abode lasts, and created in them wonders of craftsmanship and marvels of formation that are a lesson for those who take heed, is capable of creating you after your death and raising you from your graves. ﴿And the difference of your tongues﴾, that is, your languages, among Arabs and non-Arabs, Turks, Romans and other languages, ﴿and your colors﴾, of whiteness, blackness, redness, yellowness, blueness and greenness, despite your being children of one man and one mother, and despite being gathered under one species, which is humanity, and one differentia, which is rationality, until you became distinguished from one another, so that this is not confused with that, but in every individual among you there is something that distinguishes him from the other individuals. In this is a wondrous power that none understands except those who know, and none comprehends except the reflective. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who know﴾, who are of the kind of this world, without distinction between the righteous and the wicked.

The majority recited the lam of "al-'alamin" with a fatha. Hafs alone recited it with a kasra. al-Farra' said: it has a good justification, for He has said: ﴿signs for a people who understand﴾ [al-Ra'd: 4], ﴿signs for those of understanding﴾ [Al 'Imran: 190], ﴿and none understands them except those who know﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 43].

﴿And among His signs is your sleeping by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty﴾. It was said: there is inversion in the speech, and the sense is: and among His signs is your sleeping by night and your seeking of His bounty by day.

It was said: the meaning is sound without inversion, that is: and among His great signs is that you sleep by night and you sleep by day at some times for rest, like the time of qaylula (the afternoon rest), and your seeking of His bounty in both of them, for each of these contains that, though seeking bounty in the day is more frequent.

The first is what is appropriate to the other verses that occur with this meaning, and the second is what is appropriate to the Qur'anic arrangement here.

The reason for mentioning sleep and seeking here, and making them among the proofs of the resurrection, is that sleep resembles death, and the disposing of needs and striving for gains resembles life after death. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who hear﴾, that is, who hear the signs and admonitions with the hearing of one who reflects and ponders, and so they deduce from that the resurrection.

﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope﴾. The meaning: that He shows you. The "an" has been deleted because the context indicates it, as Tarafa said:

"Unquestionably, O you who blame me, let me attend the battles,
and let me witness pleasures; will you make me immortal?"

The sense is: an ahdura (that I attend), and when the particle is deleted in the verse and in the verse of poetry, its governing function is nullified. From this is the well-known proverb: "Hearing of al-Mu'aydi is better than seeing him."

It was said: it is by inversion, that is: and He shows you the lightning from among His signs, so it is a conjunction of a verbal sentence to a nominal sentence. It is permissible that "yurikum" is an adjective to a deleted noun, that is: and among His signs is a sign by which and in which He shows you the lightning. It was said: the sense is: and among His signs He shows you the lightning, as fear and as hope, from among His signs.

al-Zajjaj said: then it is the conjunction of a sentence to a sentence.

Qatadah said: "Fear for the traveller and hope for the resident." Al-Dahhak said: "Fear of thunderbolts and hope for the rain." Yahya ibn Salam said: "Fear of the hail destroying the crops, and hope for the rain to revive the crops." Ibn Bahr said: "Fear that the lightning will be dry lightning (barq khullub, lightning without rain), and hope that it will bring rain." He recited:

*Let not your lightning be dry lightning,*
*For the best lightning is that which comes with rain.*

The accusatives *khawfan* (fearing) and *tama'an* (hoping) are in the sense of purpose (*'illah*, the grammatical "cause" or reason construction). ﴿And He sends down water from the sky, and with it revives the earth after its death﴾, meaning He revives it with vegetation after it has dried up. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason﴾, for whoever has a share of intellect knows that this is a sign by which the overpowering power is proven.

﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command﴾, meaning their standing and their remaining firm is by His will, glory be to Him, and His power, without any pillar supporting them and without any place on which they rest.

Al-Farra' said: "It means that they endure standing by His command." ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come out﴾, meaning: then, after your death and your being placed in the graves, when He calls you with one call, you will come out from them immediately, without delay or hesitation, just as an obedient one responds to the call of an obeyed caller.

*Min al-ard* (from the earth) is connected to *da'a* (called), meaning He calls you from the earth in which you are, as one says, "I called him from the bottom of the valley and he came up to me." Or it is connected to an omitted word that describes *da'wah* (call). Or it is connected to an omitted word indicated by *takhrujun* (you come out), meaning: you came out from the earth. It is not permissible for it to be connected to *takhrujun*, because what follows *idha* (when) does not govern what precedes it. This call is the last blast of Israfil on the Trumpet, as its explanation has already passed. The reciters have agreed on the fatha on the *ta'* in *takhrujun* here. Whoever said it was read here with a damma, in the passive form, was mistaken; it is read with a damma only in *al-A'raf*.

﴿And to Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth﴾, from all created beings, in ownership, disposal and creation; none other has any share in that. ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾, meaning obedient in submission. It was also said: acknowledging servitude. It was said: praying. It was said: standing on the Day of Resurrection, as in His saying ﴿the Day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 6], meaning for reckoning. It was said: bearing witness that they are His servants. It was said: sincere.

﴿And it is He who begins creation, then repeats it﴾ after death, so He gives them life, an everlasting life. ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾, meaning easy for Him, He does not find it difficult. Or: "easier for Him" in comparison with your power and with what some of you say to others. Otherwise, nothing in His power is easier than another thing; rather, all things are equal to Him, and He brings them into being by His word: *kun* (be), and it is.

Abu 'Ubayd said: "Whoever takes *ahwan* (easier) as an expression of preferring one thing over another, his view is rejected by His saying ﴿And that is ever easy for Allah﴾ [an-Nisa': 169] and by His saying ﴿and their preserving them does not burden Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]." The Arabs often use the form *af'al* in the sense of *fa'il*, as in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*Indeed He who raised the sky built for us*
*A house whose pillars are mighty and tall.*

That is, *'azizah* (mighty) and *tawilah* (tall). Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab cited this as evidence:

*Men wished that I would die, and if I die,*
*That is a path in which I am not the only one.*

That is, *lastu bi-wahid* (I am not one alone). Similar is the saying of another:

*By your life, indeed al-Zibriqan is generous*
*With his kindness in hard years, and more excellent.*

That is, *wa-fadil* (and excellent). Abdullah ibn Mas'ud read *wa-huwa 'alayhi hayyin* (and it is easy for Him). Mujahid, 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the repetition is easier for Him than the beginning, that is, more facile, even though all of it is easy.

It was also said: the meaning is that re-creation among created beings is easier than the beginning. It was also said: the pronoun in *'alayhi* refers to the created beings, meaning it is easier for the creatures, because they will be called with one cry and they will stand up, and it will be said to them "Be!" and they will be. That is easier for them than becoming a drop of semen, then a clot, then a lump of flesh, through to the end of the stages of creation.

﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾. Al-Khalil said: *al-mathal* means the attribute, that is, His is the highest attribute in the heavens and the earth, as He said ﴿the likeness of Paradise which the righteous have been promised﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 35; Muhammad: 15], meaning its description. Mujahid said: the highest likeness is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and Qatadah said the same.

Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning His saying ﴿and it is easier for Him﴾, which He has set forth as an example for you concerning what is difficult and what is easy.

It was also said: the highest likeness is that there is nothing like Him. It was said: it is that whatever He wills comes to be by the word *kun* (be). *Fi al-samawati wal-ard* (in the heavens and the earth) is connected to the meaning of the preceding sentence. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, is known by the highest likeness and described by it in the heavens and the earth. It is also permissible for it to be connected to an omitted word, as a circumstantial description (*hal*) of "the highest", or of "likeness", or of the pronoun in "the highest". He is the Mighty in His dominion, the Overpowering who cannot be overcome, the Wise in His sayings and His deeds.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yublisu* (despair): he said, "it means he becomes miserable." Al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported concerning *yublisu*: "he is grieved." And from him: *al-iblas* means disgrace.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying *yuhbarun* (they will be delighted): he said, "they will be honoured." Al-Daylami reported from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will say: 'Where are those who used to keep their ears and eyes free from the flutes of Satan? Distinguish them.' They will be distinguished by heaps of musk and ambergris. Then He will say to the angels: 'Make them hear My glorification, My praise and My declaration of His oneness.' They will glorify Him with voices the like of which the hearers have never heard before."

Al-Dinawari in *al-Mujalasah* reported from Mujahid, who said: "A caller will call on the Day of Resurrection," and he mentioned something similar, but he did not name the one who narrated it to him from the Messenger of Allah.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhamm al-Malahi* and al-Isbahani in *al-Targhib* reported something similar from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya and al-Diya' al-Maqdisi, both in *Sifat al-Jannah*, reported, as al-Suyuti said, with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "In Paradise there is a tree on a trunk, such that a determined rider would take a hundred years to travel in its shade. The people of Paradise, including the people of the high chambers and others, will come out and converse in its shade. Some of them will long for and mention the amusements of the world, so Allah will send a wind from Paradise which will move that tree with every amusement that existed in the world."

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi in *Nawadir al-Usul* reported something similar from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Firyabi and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Every glorification (*tasbih*) in the Qur'an is prayer (*salah*)." 'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Abu Razin, who said: Nafi' ibn al-Azraq came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "Do you find the five prayers in the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." Then he recited ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾, the prayer of Maghrib, ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾, the prayer of Subh, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾, the prayer of 'Asr, ﴿and when you enter the noon﴾, the prayer of Zuhr. And he recited ﴿and after the prayer of 'Isha'﴾ [an-Nur: 58].

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him: "This verse has gathered the times of prayer: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening﴾ is Maghrib and 'Isha', ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ is Fajr, ﴿and in the late afternoon﴾ is 'Asr, and ﴿when you enter the noon﴾ is Zuhr."

Ahmad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wal-Layla*, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Da'awat* reported from Mu'adh ibn Anas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, the one who fulfilled [his covenant]? Because he used to say each time he entered the morning and the evening: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾." In its chain is Ibn Lahi'ah.

Abu Dawud, al-Tabarani, Ibn al-Sunni and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever says, when he enters the morning: ﴿So glorify Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and in the late afternoon and when you enter the noon﴾, and ﴿He brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living, and revives the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾, he will attain what he missed on that day. And whoever says it when he enters the evening will attain what he missed in that night." Its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿All are devoutly obedient to Him﴾: he said, "obedient," meaning in life, resurrection and death; and they are disobedient to Him in other matters of worship.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "easier (*aysar*)."

Ibn al-Anbari reported from him also, concerning His saying ﴿And it is easier for Him﴾: he said, "The repetition is easier for the created being, because He says to it on the Day of Resurrection, 'Be!' and it is. He began the creation from a drop of semen, then from a clot, then from a lump of flesh."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also reported from him concerning His saying ﴿And to Him belongs the highest likeness﴾: he said, "There is nothing like Him."

[p. 1133]

His saying: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾. The meaning of *mathal* (parable) has already been verified. The *min* in *min anfusikum* is for the beginning of the limit (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), and it, together with its genitive, is in the accusative position as a description of *mathalan*, meaning: a parable drawn and taken from yourselves, for it is the closest thing to you and clearer to you than anything else. So when He coined for you the parable of it in the invalidity of association (*shirk*), it was more evident in its indication and greater in its clarity.

Then He explained the parable mentioned, saying: ﴿Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you?﴾ The *min* in *mimma malakat* is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*), and the *min* in *min shuraka'* is extra, for emphasis. The meaning is: Do you have partners in what We have provided for you, of the kind that your right hands possess, namely the slaves and the maidservants? The interrogation is for denial, and the clause ﴿so you are equal in it﴾ is the answer to the interrogation, which carries the sense of negation, and it confirms the meaning of partnership between them and the slaves and maidservants owned by them in their wealth. That is: Would you be pleased for yourselves, while your slaves and maidservants are your equals in humanity, that they should be equal to you in disposing of what We have provided you of wealth, and share in it with you, without any distinction between you and them? ﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾. The *ka* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: you fear the free persons who resemble you in freedom, ownership of wealth, and permission to dispose of it. The intended purpose is the negation of three things: partnership between you and the owned, equality with them, and your fear of them.

It is not meant to affirm partnership and deny equality and fear, as was said regarding their saying: ﴿Why does he not come to us and speak to us?﴾ Rather, the purpose is to establish proof against the polytheists, for they must say: "We are not pleased with that." Then it is said to them: How can you deem yourselves too exalted to share with those owned by you, when they are your equals in humanity, and yet you make the servants of God partners to Him? So when partnership between slaves and their masters in what the masters own is invalidated, partnership between God and any one of His creation is invalidated as well, since all creation are servants of God, exalted is He, and nothing remains except that He alone is the Lord, with no partner.

The majority recited *anfusakum* in the accusative, as an object of the verbal noun added to its agent. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, on the basis of the verbal noun being added to its object.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs in a clear detailing and a manifest explanation for a people who use their intellect﴾, because they are the ones who benefit from the signs, both revealed and created, by using their intellects in reflecting upon them and considering them.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from addressing the polytheists and guiding them to the truth by means of the parable He had coined for them, and said: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their desires without knowledge﴾. That is: they did not use their intellect regarding the signs; rather they followed their deviant desires and their corrupt, false opinions. The position of *bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: ignorant that they are upon misguidance. ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray?﴾ That is: no one is able to guide him, because right guidance is by God's decree and will. ﴿And they have no helpers﴾, that is: those whom God has led astray have no helpers who would support them and prevent between them and the punishment of God, glory be to Him.

Then He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to affirm His oneness and worship Him, as He had commanded him, saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾. He likened the turning toward the religion to the straightening of one's face toward it and facing it. The accusative of *hanifan* is a circumstantial state either from the agent of *aqim* or from its object, meaning: inclining toward it, steadfast upon it, not turning to other false religions. ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾. *Fitrah* originally means creation (*khilqa*), and what is meant here is the creed (*milla*), which is Islam and monotheism.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the statement of the commentators regarding "the nature of God." What is meant by "mankind" here are those whom God created upon Islam, because the polytheist was not created upon Islam. Although this address is specifically to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his community is included with him in it.

Al-Qurtubi said, by consensus of the exegetes: It is preferable to take "mankind" in its generality, without distinction between their Muslims and their disbelievers, and that all of them are created upon that, were it not for accidents that befall them, by which they remain upon disbelief, as in the sound hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No child is born except upon the *fitrah*." And in another narration: "upon this creed. But his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you see in it any mutilation?" Then Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind; there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾. In another narration: "until you are the ones who slit their ears."

What has come in support of this hadith of Abu Hurayra will be mentioned at the end of the discussion. Thus every individual of mankind is created (*maftur*), that is, created upon the creed of Islam. But the innate faith and innate Islam are not taken into account; rather, legal faith and legal Islam are what is taken into account. This is the view of a group of the Companions and those after them, and the view of a group of exegetes, and it is the truth.

The view that what is meant by *fitrah* here is Islam is the position of the majority of the early scholars.

Others said: It is the origination by which God originated them, for He originated them for life and death, and for happiness and misery. In the speech of the Arabs, *al-fatir* is the originator, and this is a turn by those who hold this view toward the linguistic meaning of *fitrah*, while neglecting its legal meaning.

The legal meaning takes precedence over the linguistic meaning by the consensus of the people of the law. This does not preclude the occurrence of *fitrah* in the Qur'an or the Sunna in some places with the linguistic meaning intended, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Praise be to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], that is, their Creator and Originator; and as in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me﴾ [Ya-Sin: 22]. For there is no dispute that the linguistic meaning is this; rather, the dispute concerns the legal meaning of *fitrah*, which is what the earlier scholars mentioned, as we have explained.

The accusative of *fitrata* is as a verbal noun emphasizing the clause preceding it.

Al-Zajjaj said: *fitrata* is in the accusative in the sense of "follow the *fitrah* of God." He said: because the meaning of "so set your face toward the religion" is "follow the religion" and "follow the *fitrah* of God."

Ibn Jarir said: It is a verbal noun from the sense of "so set your face," because the meaning of that is "the *fitrah* of God by which He created mankind upon the religion." It was also said: it is in the accusative as an exhortation (*ighra'*), meaning: "Adhere to the *fitrah* of God," or "upon you is the *fitrah* of God." Abu Hayyan rejected this view and said: the word of exhortation cannot be omitted, since it is a substitute for the verb, so omitting it would entail omitting both the substitute and what it substitutes, which is a grave matter.

It is answered that this is the opinion of the Basrans, but al-Kisa'i and his followers permit it.

The clause ﴿there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the command to adhere to the *fitrah*, meaning: this *fitrah* upon which God created mankind has no alteration from the side of the Creator, glory be to Him.

It was also said: it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not alter the creation of God. Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: its meaning is: there is no alteration of the religion of God. Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: this applies to beliefs. 'Ikrima said: the meaning is that there is no changing of the creation in animals, such as by castrating their males.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, that is: that religion upon which one is commanded to set one's face is the upright religion; or adherence to the *fitrah* is the upright religion. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that until they do it and act upon it.

﴿Turning penitently to Him﴾, that is: returning to Him in repentance and sincerity, and obeying Him in His commands and prohibitions.

From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*"If they repent, then Banu Sulaym and their people, Hawazin, have indeed turned back."*

Al-Jawhari said: *anaba ila Allah* means: he turned toward God and repented. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state from the agent of *aqim*.

Al-Mubarrad said: because the meaning of "aqim wajhaka" is "aqimu wujuhakum" (establish your faces).

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so set your face and those with you turning penitently," and Al-Zajjaj said likewise, and said its estimate is: "so set your face and your community," so the circumstantial state applies to all of them.

The omission of the conjoined element is permitted because *munibin* indicates it.

It was also said: it is in the accusative as an *qat'* (detached, a change of case), and it was said: it is in the accusative because it is the predicate of an omitted *kana*, meaning: "and be turning penitently to Him," the indication being ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾.

Then, glory be to Him, commanded them to be God-fearing after commanding them to turn penitently, saying: ﴿and fear Him﴾, that is: by avoiding His disobedience. It is conjoined to the implied verb governing *munibin*. ﴿And establish the prayer which you have been commanded, and do not be among the polytheists in God.﴾

His saying: ﴿of those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ is a substitute for what precedes it, with the preposition repeated. *Shiya'* means factions, that is: do not be among those who split into factions in religion, each faction supporting the others, from among the people of innovations and desires.

It was also said: what is meant by "those who divided their religion into sects" are the Jews and the Christians.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *farraqu dinahum* (they divided their religion), and this recitation is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, meaning: they abandoned their religion, which must be followed, namely monotheism.

The interpretation of this verse has already been given at the end of Surah al-An'am: ﴿every faction rejoicing in what is with them﴾, that is: every group rejoicing and delighted in the religion they hold, which is founded on what is not correct, thinking that they are upon the truth while they possess nothing of it.

Al-Farra' said: it is permissible that His saying ﴿of those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ be a new sentence, just as it is permissible that it be connected to what precedes it.

﴿And when harm touches mankind﴾, that is: drought and hardship, they call upon their Lord to remove it from them, and they cry out to Him, turning penitently to Him, that is: returning to Him, seeking refuge in Him, relying on no one else. It was also said: turning toward Him with all their hearts. ﴿Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Him﴾, by answering their supplication and removing those hardships from them, ﴿behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord﴾. *Idha* here is the sudden *idha* (*idha al-fuja'iyya*), and it came as the answer to the condition, because it is like the *fa'* in conveying sequence, meaning: a group of them suddenly committed association, and they are the ones who had called upon Him, and He delivered them from what they were in.

This statement is brought to express wonder at their conditions, and at what they became: acknowledging the oneness of God, glory be to Him, when hardships descend, and returning to association when it is lifted from them.

The *lam* in ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*). It was said: it is the *lam* of command, for the purpose of threat and warning. It was said: it is the *lam* of consequence.

Then, glory be to Him, addressed those who had done what they had done, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ what follows this fleeting enjoyment of painful punishment.

The majority recited *fatamatta'u* in the second person. Abu al-'Aliya recited it with the *ya'* (third person) in the passive voice. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is *falyatamatta'u* (let them enjoy).

﴿Or have We sent down upon them an authority?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* (*al-munqati'a*), and the interrogation is for denial. *Sultan* means clear proof, so it "speaks" (*yatakallamu*), that is, indicates, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make *sultan* feminine; they say: "The authority has decided this against you." But the Basrans regard the masculine as more eloquent, and the Qur'an came with it, while the feminine is permissible in their view since it has the meaning of proof. It was also said: what is meant by *sultan* here is a king. ﴿Concerning what they associated with Him﴾, that is: it speaks of their associating others with God, glory be to Him. It is permissible that the *ba'* be causal, that is: because of the matter by which they associate.

﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy﴾, that is: fertility, bounty, abundance, and well-being, they rejoice in it with the joy of insolence and arrogance, not the joy of gratitude and delight at its reaching them. ﴿Say: By the grace of God and His mercy, so let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, that is, hardship, in whatever form, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, that is, because of their sins, ﴿behold, they despair.﴾ *Qunut* means despair of mercy. So said the majority.

Al-Hasan said: al-qunut is abandoning the obligations of Allah, glory be to Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaqnutun" with a damma on the nun, while Abu 'Amr, al-Kisai and Ya'qub read it with a kasra.

﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it?﴾ He widens it for whom He wills and "yaqdiru" means He constricts it for whom He wills, for a benefit in widening it for the one who is widened and in constricting it for the one who is constricted. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, who thus reason toward the truth, because they point to the perfection of power, the wondrous craftsmanship and the marvelous creation.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The people of polytheism used to say in their talbiyah:

"Here I am, O Allah, no partner is Yours, except a partner that is Yours; You own it and what it owns."

So Allah revealed: ﴿Do any of your slaves whom your right hands possess share with you in what We have provided you?﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding the verse that it refers to the deities, and in it he says: "You fear them lest they inherit from you as some of you inherit from one another."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾, he said: it is the religion of Allah. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, he said: the upright judgment.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' (p-1135) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a military expedition to Khaybar, and they fought the polytheists. The killing reached the offspring, so when they came back, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What led you to kill the offspring?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, they were only the children of polytheists." He said: "Are not the best of you only the children of polytheists? By Him in whose hand my soul is, there is no soul born except upon the fitrah until its tongue speaks for it."

Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah until his tongue expresses it; then when his tongue expresses it, either he is grateful or he is ungrateful."

Ahmad narrated it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from al-Hasan, from Jabir.

Imam Ahmad said in al-Musnad: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Hisham narrated to us, Qatadah narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from 'Iyad ibn Hammad: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once delivered a sermon, and in his sermon, relating from Allah, glory be to Him, he said: 'Indeed I created My servants as ḥunafa' (upright in faith), all of them, and the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion, and made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them.'" The hadith...

The accusative of *fitrata* is as a verbal noun emphasizing the clause preceding it.

Al-Zajjaj said: *fitrata* is in the accusative in the sense of "follow the *fitrah* of God." He said: because the meaning of "so set your face toward the religion" is "follow the religion" and "follow the *fitrah* of God."

Ibn Jarir said: It is a verbal noun from the sense of "so set your face," because the meaning of that is "the *fitrah* of God by which He created mankind upon the religion." It was also said: it is in the accusative as an exhortation (*ighra'*), meaning: "Adhere to the *fitrah* of God," or "upon you is the *fitrah* of God." Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: its meaning is: there is no alteration of the religion of God. Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: this applies to beliefs. 'Ikrima said: the meaning is that there is no changing of the creation in animals, such as by castrating their males.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, that is: that religion upon which one is commanded to set one's face is the upright religion; or adherence to the *fitrah* is the upright religion. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that until they do it and act upon it.

﴿Turning penitently to Him﴾, that is: returning to Him in repentance and sincerity, and obeying Him in His commands and prohibitions.

From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

His saying: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾. The meaning of *mathal* (parable) has already been verified. The *min* in *min anfusikum* is for the beginning of the limit (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), and it, together with its genitive, is in the accusative position as a description of *mathalan*, meaning: a parable drawn and taken from yourselves, for it is the closest thing to you and clearer to you than anything else. So when He coined for you the parable of it in the invalidity of association (*shirk*), it was more evident in its indication and greater in its clarity.

Then He explained the parable mentioned, saying: ﴿Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you?﴾ The *min* in *mimma malakat* is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*), and the *min* in *min shuraka'* is extra, for emphasis. The meaning is: Do you have partners in what We have provided for you, of the kind that your right hands possess, namely the slaves and the maidservants? The interrogation is for denial, and the clause ﴿so you are equal in it﴾ is the answer to the interrogation, which carries the sense of negation, and it confirms the meaning of partnership between them and the slaves and maidservants owned by them in their wealth. That is: Would you be pleased for yourselves, while your slaves and maidservants are your equals in humanity, that they should be equal to you in disposing of what We have provided you of wealth, and share in it with you, without any distinction between you and them? ﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾. The *ka* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: you fear the free persons who resemble you in freedom, ownership of wealth, and permission to dispose of it. The intended purpose is the negation of three things: partnership between you and the owned, equality with them, and your fear of them.

It is not meant to affirm partnership and deny equality and fear, as was said regarding their saying: ﴿Why does he not come to us and speak to us?﴾ Rather, the purpose is to establish proof against the polytheists, for they must say: "We are not pleased with that." Then it is said to them: How can you deem yourselves too exalted to share with those owned by you, when they are your equals in humanity, and yet you make the servants of God partners to Him? So when partnership between slaves and their masters in what the masters own is invalidated, partnership between God and any one of His creation is invalidated as well, since all creation are servants of God, exalted is He, and nothing remains except that He alone is the Lord, with no partner.

The majority recited *anfusakum* in the accusative, as an object of the verbal noun added to its agent. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, on the basis of the verbal noun being added to its object.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs in a clear detailing and a manifest explanation for a people who use their intellect﴾, because they are the ones who benefit from the signs, both revealed and created, by using their intellects in reflecting upon them and considering them.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs in a clear detailing and a manifest explanation for a people who use their intellect﴾, because they are the ones who benefit from the signs, both revealed and created, by using their intellects in reflecting upon them and considering them.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from addressing the polytheists and guiding them to the truth by means of the parable He had coined for them, and said: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their desires without knowledge﴾. That is: they did not use their intellect regarding the signs; rather they followed their deviant desires and their corrupt, false opinions. The position of *bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: ignorant that they are upon misguidance. ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray?﴾ That is: no one is able to guide him, because right guidance is by God's decree and will. ﴿And they have no helpers﴾, that is: those whom God has led astray have no helpers who would support them and prevent between them and the punishment of God, glory be to Him.

Then He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to affirm His oneness and worship Him, as He had commanded him, saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾. He likened the turning toward the religion to the straightening of one's face toward it and facing it. The accusative of *hanifan* is a circumstantial state either from the agent of *aqim* or from its object, meaning: inclining toward it, steadfast upon it, not turning to other false religions. ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾. *Fitrah* originally means creation (*khilqa*), and what is meant here is the creed (*milla*), which is Islam and monotheism.

Then Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind; there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾. In another narration: "until you are the ones who slit their ears."

What has come in support of this hadith of Abu Hurayra will be mentioned at the end of the discussion. The accusative of *fitrata* is as a verbal noun emphasizing the clause preceding it.

Ibn Jarir said: It is a verbal noun from the sense of "so set your face," because the meaning of that is "the *fitrah* of God by which He created mankind upon the religion." It was also said: it is in the accusative as an exhortation (*ighra'*), meaning: "Adhere to the *fitrah* of God," or "upon you is the *fitrah* of God." It is answered that this is the opinion of the Basrans, but al-Kisa'i and his followers permit it.

It was also said: it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not alter the creation of God. Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: its meaning is: there is no alteration of the religion of God. Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: this applies to beliefs. 'Ikrima said: the meaning is that there is no changing of the creation in animals, such as by castrating their males.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, that is: that religion upon which one is commanded to set one's face is the upright religion; or adherence to the *fitrah* is the upright religion. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that until they do it and act upon it.

﴿Turning penitently to Him﴾, that is: returning to Him in repentance and sincerity, and obeying Him in His commands and prohibitions.

From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*"If they repent, then Banu Sulaym and their people, Hawazin, have indeed turned back."*

Al-Jawhari said: *anaba ila Allah* means: he turned toward God and repented. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state from the agent of *aqim*.

Al-Mubarrad said: because the meaning of "aqim wajhaka" is "aqimu wujuhakum" (establish your faces).

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so set your face and those with you turning penitently," and Al-Zajjaj said likewise, and said its estimate is: "so set your face and your community," so the circumstantial state applies to all of them.

The omission of the conjoined element is permitted because *munibin* indicates it.

It was also said: it is in the accusative as an *qat'* (detached, a change of case), and it was said: it is in the accusative because it is the predicate of an omitted *kana*, meaning: "and be turning penitently to Him," the indication being ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾.

Then, glory be to Him, commanded them to be God-fearing after commanding them to turn penitently, saying: ﴿and fear Him﴾, that is: by avoiding His disobedience. It is conjoined to the implied verb governing *munibin*. ﴿And establish the prayer which you have been commanded, and do not be among the polytheists in God.﴾

His saying: ﴿of those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ is a substitute for what precedes it, with the preposition repeated. *Shiya'* means factions, that is: do not be among those who split into factions in religion, each faction supporting the others, from among the people of innovations and desires.

It was also said: what is meant by "those who divided their religion into sects" are the Jews and the Christians.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *farraqu dinahum* (they divided their religion), and this recitation is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, meaning: they abandoned their religion, which must be followed, namely monotheism.

Al-Farra' said: it is permissible that His saying ﴿of those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ be a new sentence, just as it is permissible that it be connected to what precedes it.

﴿And when harm touches mankind﴾, that is: drought and hardship, they call upon their Lord to remove it from them, and they cry out to Him, turning penitently to Him, that is: returning to Him, seeking refuge in Him, relying on no one else. It was also said: turning toward Him with all their hearts. ﴿Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Him﴾, by answering their supplication and removing those hardships from them, ﴿behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord﴾. *Idha* here is the sudden *idha* (*idha al-fuja'iyya*), and it came as the answer to the condition, because it is like the *fa'* in conveying sequence, meaning: a group of them suddenly committed association, and they are the ones who had called upon Him, and He delivered them from what they were in.

This statement is brought to express wonder at their conditions, and at what they became: acknowledging the oneness of God, glory be to Him, when hardships descend, and returning to association when it is lifted from them.

The *lam* in ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*). It was said: it is the *lam* of command, for the purpose of threat and warning. It was said: it is the *lam* of consequence.

Then, glory be to Him, addressed those who had done what they had done, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ what follows this fleeting enjoyment of painful punishment.

The majority recited *fatamatta'u* in the second person. Abu al-'Aliya recited it with the *ya'* (third person) in the passive voice. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is *falyatamatta'u* (let them enjoy).

﴿Or have We sent down upon them an authority?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* (*al-munqati'a*), and the interrogation is for denial. *Sultan* means clear proof, so it "speaks" (*yatakallamu*), that is, indicates, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. But the Basrans regard the masculine as more eloquent, and the Qur'an came with it, while the feminine is permissible in their view since it has the meaning of proof. It was also said: what is meant by *sultan* here is a king. ﴿Concerning what they associated with Him﴾, that is: it speaks of their associating others with God, glory be to Him. It is permissible that the *ba'* be causal, that is: because of the matter by which they associate.

﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy﴾, that is: fertility, bounty, abundance, and well-being, they rejoice in it with the joy of insolence and arrogance, not the joy of gratitude and delight at its reaching them. ﴿Say: By the grace of God and His mercy, so let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, that is, hardship, in whatever form, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, that is, because of their sins, ﴿behold, they despair.﴾ *Qunut* means despair of mercy. So said the majority.

Al-Hasan said: al-qunut is abandoning the obligations of Allah, glory be to Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaqnutun" with a damma on the nun, while Abu 'Amr, al-Kisai and Ya'qub read it with a kasra.

﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it?﴾ He widens it for whom He wills and "yaqdiru" means He constricts it for whom He wills, for a benefit in widening it for the one who is widened and in constricting it for the one who is constricted. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, who thus reason toward the truth, because they point to the perfection of power, the wondrous craftsmanship and the marvelous creation.

So Allah revealed: ﴿Do any of your slaves whom your right hands possess share with you in what We have provided you?﴾, the verse.

﴿And when harm touches mankind﴾, that is: drought and hardship, they call upon their Lord to remove it from them, and they cry out to Him, turning penitently to Him, that is: returning to Him, seeking refuge in Him, relying on no one else. It was also said: turning toward Him with all their hearts. ﴿Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Him﴾, by answering their supplication and removing those hardships from them, ﴿behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord﴾. *Idha* here is the sudden *idha* (*idha al-fuja'iyya*), and it came as the answer to the condition, because it is like the *fa'* in conveying sequence, meaning: a group of them suddenly committed association, and they are the ones who had called upon Him, and He delivered them from what they were in.

This statement is brought to express wonder at their conditions, and at what they became: acknowledging the oneness of God, glory be to Him, when hardships descend, and returning to association when it is lifted from them.

The *lam* in ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*). It was said: it is the *lam* of command, for the purpose of threat and warning. It was said: it is the *lam* of consequence.

Then, glory be to Him, addressed those who had done what they had done, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ what follows this fleeting enjoyment of painful punishment.

The majority recited *fatamatta'u* in the second person. Abu al-'Aliya recited it with the *ya'* (third person) in the passive voice. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is *falyatamatta'u* (let them enjoy).

﴿Or have We sent down upon them an authority?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* (*al-munqati'a*), and the interrogation is for denial. *Sultan* means clear proof, so it "speaks" (*yatakallamu*), that is, indicates, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make *sultan* feminine; they say: "The authority has decided this against you." But the Basrans regard the masculine as more eloquent, and the Qur'an came with it, while the feminine is permissible in their view since it has the meaning of proof. It is permissible that the *ba'* be causal, that is: because of the matter by which they associate.

So said the majority.

Al-Hasan said: al-qunut is abandoning the obligations of Allah, glory be to Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaqnutun" with a damma on the nun, while Abu 'Amr, al-Kisai and Ya'qub read it with a kasra.

So Allah revealed: ﴿Do any of your slaves whom your right hands possess share with you in what We have provided you?﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding the verse that it refers to the deities, and in it he says: "You fear them lest they inherit from you as some of you inherit from one another."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾, he said: it is the religion of Allah. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, he said: the upright judgment.

His saying: ﴿He has coined for you a parable from yourselves﴾. The meaning of *mathal* (parable) has already been verified. The *min* in *min anfusikum* is for the beginning of the limit (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), and it, together with its genitive, is in the accusative position as a description of *mathalan*, meaning: a parable drawn and taken from yourselves, for it is the closest thing to you and clearer to you than anything else. So when He coined for you the parable of it in the invalidity of association (*shirk*), it was more evident in its indication and greater in its clarity.

Then He explained the parable mentioned, saying: ﴿Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you?﴾ The *min* in *mimma malakat* is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*), and the *min* in *min shuraka'* is extra, for emphasis. The meaning is: Do you have partners in what We have provided for you, of the kind that your right hands possess, namely the slaves and the maidservants? The interrogation is for denial, and the clause ﴿so you are equal in it﴾ is the answer to the interrogation, which carries the sense of negation, and it confirms the meaning of partnership between them and the slaves and maidservants owned by them in their wealth. That is: Would you be pleased for yourselves, while your slaves and maidservants are your equals in humanity, that they should be equal to you in disposing of what We have provided you of wealth, and share in it with you, without any distinction between you and them? ﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾. The *ka* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: you fear the free persons who resemble you in freedom, ownership of wealth, and permission to dispose of it. The intended purpose is the negation of three things: partnership between you and the owned, equality with them, and your fear of them.

It is not meant to affirm partnership and deny equality and fear, as was said regarding their saying: ﴿Why does he not come to us and speak to us?﴾ Rather, the purpose is to establish proof against the polytheists, for they must say: "We are not pleased with that." Then it is said to them: How can you deem yourselves too exalted to share with those owned by you, when they are your equals in humanity, and yet you make the servants of God partners to Him? So when partnership between slaves and their masters in what the masters own is invalidated, partnership between God and any one of His creation is invalidated as well, since all creation are servants of God, exalted is He, and nothing remains except that He alone is the Lord, with no partner.

The majority recited *anfusakum* in the accusative, as an object of the verbal noun added to its agent. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, on the basis of the verbal noun being added to its object.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs in a clear detailing and a manifest explanation for a people who use their intellect﴾, because they are the ones who benefit from the signs, both revealed and created, by using their intellects in reflecting upon them and considering them.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from addressing the polytheists and guiding them to the truth by means of the parable He had coined for them, and said: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their desires without knowledge﴾. That is: they did not use their intellect regarding the signs; rather they followed their deviant desires and their corrupt, false opinions. The position of *bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: ignorant that they are upon misguidance. ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray?﴾ That is: no one is able to guide him, because right guidance is by God's decree and will. ﴿And they have no helpers﴾, that is: those whom God has led astray have no helpers who would support them and prevent between them and the punishment of God, glory be to Him.

Then He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to affirm His oneness and worship Him, as He had commanded him, saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾. He likened the turning toward the religion to the straightening of one's face toward it and facing it. The accusative of *hanifan* is a circumstantial state either from the agent of *aqim* or from its object, meaning: inclining toward it, steadfast upon it, not turning to other false religions. ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾. *Fitrah* originally means creation (*khilqa*), and what is meant here is the creed (*milla*), which is Islam and monotheism.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the statement of the commentators regarding "the nature of God." What is meant by "mankind" here are those whom God created upon Islam, because the polytheist was not created upon Islam. Although this address is specifically to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his community is included with him in it.

Al-Qurtubi said, by consensus of the exegetes: It is preferable to take "mankind" in its generality, without distinction between their Muslims and their disbelievers, and that all of them are created upon that, were it not for accidents that befall them, by which they remain upon disbelief, as in the sound hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No child is born except upon the *fitrah*." Then Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind; there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾. In another narration: "until you are the ones who slit their ears."

What has come in support of this hadith of Abu Hurayra will be mentioned at the end of the discussion. Thus every individual of mankind is created (*maftur*), that is, created upon the creed of Islam. But the innate faith and innate Islam are not taken into account; rather, legal faith and legal Islam are what is taken into account. This is the view of a group of the Companions and those after them, and the view of a group of exegetes, and it is the truth.

The view that what is meant by *fitrah* here is Islam is the position of the majority of the early scholars.

Others said: It is the origination by which God originated them, for He originated them for life and death, and for happiness and misery. In the speech of the Arabs, *al-fatir* is the originator, and this is a turn by those who hold this view toward the linguistic meaning of *fitrah*, while neglecting its legal meaning.

The legal meaning takes precedence over the linguistic meaning by the consensus of the people of the law. This does not preclude the occurrence of *fitrah* in the Qur'an or the Sunna in some places with the linguistic meaning intended, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Praise be to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], that is, their Creator and Originator; and as in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me﴾ [Ya-Sin: 22]. For there is no dispute that the linguistic meaning is this; rather, the dispute concerns the legal meaning of *fitrah*, which is what the earlier scholars mentioned, as we have explained.

The accusative of *fitrata* is as a verbal noun emphasizing the clause preceding it.

Al-Zajjaj said: *fitrata* is in the accusative in the sense of "follow the *fitrah* of God." He said: because the meaning of "so set your face toward the religion" is "follow the religion" and "follow the *fitrah* of God."

Ibn Jarir said: It is a verbal noun from the sense of "so set your face," because the meaning of that is "the *fitrah* of God by which He created mankind upon the religion." It was also said: it is in the accusative as an exhortation (*ighra'*), meaning: "Adhere to the *fitrah* of God," or "upon you is the *fitrah* of God." Abu Hayyan rejected this view and said: the word of exhortation cannot be omitted, since it is a substitute for the verb, so omitting it would entail omitting both the substitute and what it substitutes, which is a grave matter.

It is answered that this is the opinion of the Basrans, but al-Kisa'i and his followers permit it.

The clause ﴿there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the command to adhere to the *fitrah*, meaning: this *fitrah* upon which God created mankind has no alteration from the side of the Creator, glory be to Him.

It was also said: it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not alter the creation of God. Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: its meaning is: there is no alteration of the religion of God. Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: this applies to beliefs. 'Ikrima said: the meaning is that there is no changing of the creation in animals, such as by castrating their males.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, that is: that religion upon which one is commanded to set one's face is the upright religion; or adherence to the *fitrah* is the upright religion. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that until they do it and act upon it.

﴿Turning penitently to Him﴾, that is: returning to Him in repentance and sincerity, and obeying Him in His commands and prohibitions.

From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*"If they repent, then Banu Sulaym and their people, Hawazin, have indeed turned back."*

Al-Jawhari said: *anaba ila Allah* means: he turned toward God and repented. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state from the agent of *aqim*.

Al-Mubarrad said: because the meaning of "aqim wajhaka" is "aqimu wujuhakum" (establish your faces).

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so set your face and those with you turning penitently," and Al-Zajjaj said likewise, and said its estimate is: "so set your face and your community," so the circumstantial state applies to all of them.

The omission of the conjoined element is permitted because *munibin* indicates it.

It was also said: it is in the accusative as an *qat'* (detached, a change of case), and it was said: it is in the accusative because it is the predicate of an omitted *kana*, meaning: "and be turning penitently to Him," the indication being ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾.

Then, glory be to Him, commanded them to be God-fearing after commanding them to turn penitently, saying: ﴿and fear Him﴾, that is: by avoiding His disobedience. The accusative of *fitrata* is as a verbal noun emphasizing the clause preceding it.

So when He coined for you the parable of it in the invalidity of association (*shirk*), it was more evident in its indication and greater in its clarity.

Then He explained the parable mentioned, saying: ﴿Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you?﴾ The *min* in *mimma malakat* is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*), and the *min* in *min shuraka'* is extra, for emphasis. The meaning is: Do you have partners in what We have provided for you, of the kind that your right hands possess, namely the slaves and the maidservants? The interrogation is for denial, and the clause ﴿so you are equal in it﴾ is the answer to the interrogation, which carries the sense of negation, and it confirms the meaning of partnership between them and the slaves and maidservants owned by them in their wealth. That is: Would you be pleased for yourselves, while your slaves and maidservants are your equals in humanity, that they should be equal to you in disposing of what We have provided you of wealth, and share in it with you, without any distinction between you and them? ﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾. The *ka* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: you fear the free persons who resemble you in freedom, ownership of wealth, and permission to dispose of it. The intended purpose is the negation of three things: partnership between you and the owned, equality with them, and your fear of them.

It is not meant to affirm partnership and deny equality and fear, as was said regarding their saying: ﴿Why does he not come to us and speak to us?﴾ Rather, the purpose is to establish proof against the polytheists, for they must say: "We are not pleased with that." Then it is said to them: How can you deem yourselves too exalted to share with those owned by you, when they are your equals in humanity, and yet you make the servants of God partners to Him? So when partnership between slaves and their masters in what the masters own is invalidated, partnership between God and any one of His creation is invalidated as well, since all creation are servants of God, exalted is He, and nothing remains except that He alone is the Lord, with no partner.
