The *min* in *min anfusikum* is for the beginning of the limit (*ibtida' al-ghaya*), and it, together with its genitive, is in the accusative position as a description of *mathalan*, meaning: a parable drawn and taken from yourselves, for it is the closest thing to you and clearer to you than anything else. So when He coined for you the parable of it in the invalidity of association (*shirk*), it was more evident in its indication and greater in its clarity.

Then He explained the parable mentioned, saying: ﴿Do you have, among what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you?﴾ The *min* in *mimma malakat* is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*), and the *min* in *min shuraka'* is extra, for emphasis. The meaning is: Do you have partners in what We have provided for you, of the kind that your right hands possess, namely the slaves and the maidservants? The interrogation is for denial, and the clause ﴿so you are equal in it﴾ is the answer to the interrogation, which carries the sense of negation, and it confirms the meaning of partnership between them and the slaves and maidservants owned by them in their wealth. That is: Would you be pleased for yourselves, while your slaves and maidservants are your equals in humanity, that they should be equal to you in disposing of what We have provided you of wealth, and share in it with you, without any distinction between you and them? ﴿You fear them as you fear one another﴾. The *ka* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: you fear the free persons who resemble you in freedom, ownership of wealth, and permission to dispose of it. The intended purpose is the negation of three things: partnership between you and the owned, equality with them, and your fear of them.

It is not meant to affirm partnership and deny equality and fear, as was said regarding their saying: ﴿Why does he not come to us and speak to us?﴾ Rather, the purpose is to establish proof against the polytheists, for they must say: "We are not pleased with that." Then it is said to them: How can you deem yourselves too exalted to share with those owned by you, when they are your equals in humanity, and yet you make the servants of God partners to Him? So when partnership between slaves and their masters in what the masters own is invalidated, partnership between God and any one of His creation is invalidated as well, since all creation are servants of God, exalted is He, and nothing remains except that He alone is the Lord, with no partner.

The majority recited *anfusakum* in the accusative, as an object of the verbal noun added to its agent. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited it in the nominative, on the basis of the verbal noun being added to its object.

﴿Thus do We detail the signs in a clear detailing and a manifest explanation for a people who use their intellect﴾, because they are the ones who benefit from the signs, both revealed and created, by using their intellects in reflecting upon them and considering them.

Then He, glory be to Him, turned away from addressing the polytheists and guiding them to the truth by means of the parable He had coined for them, and said: ﴿Rather, those who did wrong follow their desires without knowledge﴾. That is: they did not use their intellect regarding the signs; rather they followed their deviant desires and their corrupt, false opinions. The position of *bi-ghayri 'ilm* (without knowledge) is accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning: ignorant that they are upon misguidance. ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray?﴾ That is: no one is able to guide him, because right guidance is by God's decree and will. ﴿And they have no helpers﴾, that is: those whom God has led astray have no helpers who would support them and prevent between them and the punishment of God, glory be to Him.

Then He commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to affirm His oneness and worship Him, as He had commanded him, saying: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾. He likened the turning toward the religion to the straightening of one's face toward it and facing it. The accusative of *hanifan* is a circumstantial state either from the agent of *aqim* or from its object, meaning: inclining toward it, steadfast upon it, not turning to other false religions. ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind﴾. *Fitrah* originally means creation (*khilqa*), and what is meant here is the creed (*milla*), which is Islam and monotheism.

Al-Wahidi said: This is the statement of the commentators regarding "the nature of God." What is meant by "mankind" here are those whom God created upon Islam, because the polytheist was not created upon Islam. Although this address is specifically to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), his community is included with him in it.

Al-Qurtubi said, by consensus of the exegetes: It is preferable to take "mankind" in its generality, without distinction between their Muslims and their disbelievers, and that all of them are created upon that, were it not for accidents that befall them, by which they remain upon disbelief, as in the sound hadith of Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "No child is born except upon the *fitrah*." And in another narration: "upon this creed. But his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you see in it any mutilation?" Then Abu Hurayra said: Recite if you wish: ﴿The nature of God upon which He created mankind; there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾. In another narration: "until you are the ones who slit their ears."

What has come in support of this hadith of Abu Hurayra will be mentioned at the end of the discussion. Thus every individual of mankind is created (*maftur*), that is, created upon the creed of Islam. But the innate faith and innate Islam are not taken into account; rather, legal faith and legal Islam are what is taken into account. This is the view of a group of the Companions and those after them, and the view of a group of exegetes, and it is the truth.

The view that what is meant by *fitrah* here is Islam is the position of the majority of the early scholars.

Others said: It is the origination by which God originated them, for He originated them for life and death, and for happiness and misery. In the speech of the Arabs, *al-fatir* is the originator, and this is a turn by those who hold this view toward the linguistic meaning of *fitrah*, while neglecting its legal meaning.

The legal meaning takes precedence over the linguistic meaning by the consensus of the people of the law. This does not preclude the occurrence of *fitrah* in the Qur'an or the Sunna in some places with the linguistic meaning intended, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Praise be to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾ [Fatir: 1], that is, their Creator and Originator; and as in His saying: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me﴾ [Ya-Sin: 22]. For there is no dispute that the linguistic meaning is this; rather, the dispute concerns the legal meaning of *fitrah*, which is what the earlier scholars mentioned, as we have explained.

The accusative of *fitrata* is as a verbal noun emphasizing the clause preceding it.

Al-Zajjaj said: *fitrata* is in the accusative in the sense of "follow the *fitrah* of God." He said: because the meaning of "so set your face toward the religion" is "follow the religion" and "follow the *fitrah* of God."

Ibn Jarir said: It is a verbal noun from the sense of "so set your face," because the meaning of that is "the *fitrah* of God by which He created mankind upon the religion." It was also said: it is in the accusative as an exhortation (*ighra'*), meaning: "Adhere to the *fitrah* of God," or "upon you is the *fitrah* of God." Abu Hayyan rejected this view and said: the word of exhortation cannot be omitted, since it is a substitute for the verb, so omitting it would entail omitting both the substitute and what it substitutes, which is a grave matter.

It is answered that this is the opinion of the Basrans, but al-Kisa'i and his followers permit it.

The clause ﴿there is no alteration in the creation of God﴾ is a justification for what precedes it, namely the command to adhere to the *fitrah*, meaning: this *fitrah* upon which God created mankind has no alteration from the side of the Creator, glory be to Him.

It was also said: it is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: do not alter the creation of God. Mujahid and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: its meaning is: there is no alteration of the religion of God. Qatada, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: this applies to beliefs. 'Ikrima said: the meaning is that there is no changing of the creation in animals, such as by castrating their males.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾, that is: that religion upon which one is commanded to set one's face is the upright religion; or adherence to the *fitrah* is the upright religion. ﴿But most people do not know﴾ that until they do it and act upon it.

﴿Turning penitently to Him﴾, that is: returning to Him in repentance and sincerity, and obeying Him in His commands and prohibitions.

From this is the saying of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

*"If they repent, then Banu Sulaym and their people, Hawazin, have indeed turned back."*

Al-Jawhari said: *anaba ila Allah* means: he turned toward God and repented. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state from the agent of *aqim*.

Al-Mubarrad said: because the meaning of "aqim wajhaka" is "aqimu wujuhakum" (establish your faces).

Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "so set your face and those with you turning penitently," and Al-Zajjaj said likewise, and said its estimate is: "so set your face and your community," so the circumstantial state applies to all of them.

The omission of the conjoined element is permitted because *munibin* indicates it.

It was also said: it is in the accusative as an *qat'* (detached, a change of case), and it was said: it is in the accusative because it is the predicate of an omitted *kana*, meaning: "and be turning penitently to Him," the indication being ﴿and do not be among the polytheists﴾.

Then, glory be to Him, commanded them to be God-fearing after commanding them to turn penitently, saying: ﴿and fear Him﴾, that is: by avoiding His disobedience. It is conjoined to the implied verb governing *munibin*. ﴿And establish the prayer which you have been commanded, and do not be among the polytheists in God.﴾

His saying: ﴿of those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ is a substitute for what precedes it, with the preposition repeated. *Shiya'* means factions, that is: do not be among those who split into factions in religion, each faction supporting the others, from among the people of innovations and desires.

It was also said: what is meant by "those who divided their religion into sects" are the Jews and the Christians.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *farraqu dinahum* (they divided their religion), and this recitation is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, meaning: they abandoned their religion, which must be followed, namely monotheism.

The interpretation of this verse has already been given at the end of Surah al-An'am: ﴿every faction rejoicing in what is with them﴾, that is: every group rejoicing and delighted in the religion they hold, which is founded on what is not correct, thinking that they are upon the truth while they possess nothing of it.

Al-Farra' said: it is permissible that His saying ﴿of those who divided their religion and became sects﴾ be a new sentence, just as it is permissible that it be connected to what precedes it.

﴿And when harm touches mankind﴾, that is: drought and hardship, they call upon their Lord to remove it from them, and they cry out to Him, turning penitently to Him, that is: returning to Him, seeking refuge in Him, relying on no one else. It was also said: turning toward Him with all their hearts. ﴿Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Him﴾, by answering their supplication and removing those hardships from them, ﴿behold, a group of them associate others with their Lord﴾. *Idha* here is the sudden *idha* (*idha al-fuja'iyya*), and it came as the answer to the condition, because it is like the *fa'* in conveying sequence, meaning: a group of them suddenly committed association, and they are the ones who had called upon Him, and He delivered them from what they were in.

This statement is brought to express wonder at their conditions, and at what they became: acknowledging the oneness of God, glory be to Him, when hardships descend, and returning to association when it is lifted from them.

The *lam* in ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*). It was said: it is the *lam* of command, for the purpose of threat and warning. It was said: it is the *lam* of consequence.

Then, glory be to Him, addressed those who had done what they had done, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ what follows this fleeting enjoyment of painful punishment.

The majority recited *fatamatta'u* in the second person. Abu al-'Aliya recited it with the *ya'* (third person) in the passive voice. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is *falyatamatta'u* (let them enjoy).

﴿Or have We sent down upon them an authority?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* (*al-munqati'a*), and the interrogation is for denial. *Sultan* means clear proof, so it "speaks" (*yatakallamu*), that is, indicates, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make *sultan* feminine; they say: "The authority has decided this against you." But the Basrans regard the masculine as more eloquent, and the Qur'an came with it, while the feminine is permissible in their view since it has the meaning of proof. It was also said: what is meant by *sultan* here is a king. ﴿Concerning what they associated with Him﴾, that is: it speaks of their associating others with God, glory be to Him. It is permissible that the *ba'* be causal, that is: because of the matter by which they associate.

﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy﴾, that is: fertility, bounty, abundance, and well-being, they rejoice in it with the joy of insolence and arrogance, not the joy of gratitude and delight at its reaching them. ﴿Say: By the grace of God and His mercy, so let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, that is, hardship, in whatever form, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, that is, because of their sins, ﴿behold, they despair.﴾ *Qunut* means despair of mercy. So said the majority.

Al-Hasan said: al-qunut is abandoning the obligations of Allah, glory be to Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaqnutun" with a damma on the nun, while Abu 'Amr, al-Kisai and Ya'qub read it with a kasra.

﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it?﴾ He widens it for whom He wills and "yaqdiru" means He constricts it for whom He wills, for a benefit in widening it for the one who is widened and in constricting it for the one who is constricted. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, who thus reason toward the truth, because they point to the perfection of power, the wondrous craftsmanship and the marvelous creation.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The people of polytheism used to say in their talbiyah:

"Here I am, O Allah, no partner is Yours, except a partner that is Yours; You own it and what it owns."

So Allah revealed: ﴿Do any of your slaves whom your right hands possess share with you in what We have provided you?﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding the verse that it refers to the deities, and in it he says: "You fear them lest they inherit from you as some of you inherit from one another."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾, he said: it is the religion of Allah. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, he said: the upright judgment.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' (p-1135) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a military expedition to Khaybar, and they fought the polytheists. The killing reached the offspring, so when they came back, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What led you to kill the offspring?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, they were only the children of polytheists." He said: "Are not the best of you only the children of polytheists? By Him in whose hand my soul is, there is no soul born except upon the fitrah until its tongue speaks for it."

Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah until his tongue expresses it; then when his tongue expresses it, either he is grateful or he is ungrateful."

Ahmad narrated it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from al-Hasan, from Jabir.

Imam Ahmad said in al-Musnad: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Hisham narrated to us, Qatadah narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from 'Iyad ibn Hammad: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once delivered a sermon, and in his sermon, relating from Allah, glory be to Him, he said: 'Indeed I created My servants as ḥunafa' (upright in faith), all of them, and the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion, and made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them.'" The *lam* in ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾ is the *lam* of purpose (*lam kay*). It was said: it is the *lam* of command, for the purpose of threat and warning. It was said: it is the *lam* of consequence.

Then, glory be to Him, addressed those who had done what they had done, saying: ﴿So enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ what follows this fleeting enjoyment of painful punishment.

The majority recited *fatamatta'u* in the second person. Abu al-'Aliya recited it with the *ya'* (third person) in the passive voice. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is *falyatamatta'u* (let them enjoy).

﴿Or have We sent down upon them an authority?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am* (*al-munqati'a*), and the interrogation is for denial. *Sultan* means clear proof, so it "speaks" (*yatakallamu*), that is, indicates, as in His saying: ﴿This Our Book speaks against you with the truth﴾ [al-Jathiya: 29]. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs make *sultan* feminine; they say: "The authority has decided this against you." But the Basrans regard the masculine as more eloquent, and the Qur'an came with it, while the feminine is permissible in their view since it has the meaning of proof. It was also said: what is meant by *sultan* here is a king. ﴿Concerning what they associated with Him﴾, that is: it speaks of their associating others with God, glory be to Him. It is permissible that the *ba'* be causal, that is: because of the matter by which they associate.

﴿And when We let mankind taste mercy﴾, that is: fertility, bounty, abundance, and well-being, they rejoice in it with the joy of insolence and arrogance, not the joy of gratitude and delight at its reaching them. ﴿Say: By the grace of God and His mercy, so let them rejoice﴾ [Yunus: 58]. Then He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And if an evil befalls them﴾, that is, hardship, in whatever form, ﴿because of what their hands have sent forth﴾, that is, because of their sins, ﴿behold, they despair.﴾ *Qunut* means despair of mercy. So said the majority.

Al-Hasan said: al-qunut is abandoning the obligations of Allah, glory be to Him.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yaqnutun" with a damma on the nun, while Abu 'Amr, al-Kisai and Ya'qub read it with a kasra.

﴿Have they not seen that Allah extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it?﴾ He widens it for whom He wills and "yaqdiru" means He constricts it for whom He wills, for a benefit in widening it for the one who is widened and in constricting it for the one who is constricted. ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for a people who believe﴾, who thus reason toward the truth, because they point to the perfection of power, the wondrous craftsmanship and the marvelous creation.

Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: The people of polytheism used to say in their talbiyah:

"Here I am, O Allah, no partner is Yours, except a partner that is Yours; You own it and what it owns."

So Allah revealed: ﴿Do any of your slaves whom your right hands possess share with you in what We have provided you?﴾, the verse.

Ibn Jarir narrated from him regarding the verse that it refers to the deities, and in it he says: "You fear them lest they inherit from you as some of you inherit from one another."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him also, regarding His words ﴿There is no alteration in the creation of Allah﴾, he said: it is the religion of Allah. ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, he said: the upright judgment.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Aswad ibn Sari' (p-1135) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a military expedition to Khaybar, and they fought the polytheists. The killing reached the offspring, so when they came back, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "What led you to kill the offspring?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, they were only the children of polytheists." He said: "Are not the best of you only the children of polytheists? By Him in whose hand my soul is, there is no soul born except upon the fitrah until its tongue speaks for it."

Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah until his tongue expresses it; then when his tongue expresses it, either he is grateful or he is ungrateful."

Ahmad narrated it from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, from al-Hasan, from Jabir.

Imam Ahmad said in al-Musnad: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, Hisham narrated to us, Qatadah narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from 'Iyad ibn Hammad: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once delivered a sermon, and in his sermon, relating from Allah, glory be to Him, he said: 'Indeed I created My servants as ḥunafa' (upright in faith), all of them, and the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion, and made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them.'" The hadith...

When Allah, glorified is He, explained how the command of Allah should be honored, He pointed to what is due in support of kin and those in need, from among those whom Allah has granted abundance in provision. So He said: ﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community, who follow him in this, or to every responsible person who has wealth that Allah has made abundant for him. He gave precedence to kindness toward relatives, because the best charity is that given to a near relative. It is a charity that is multiplied, and it is also the maintaining of ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim), which is recommended. What is meant is kindness toward them through charity, maintaining ties, and righteousness. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾, meaning: give the needy and the wayfarer their right, which they deserve.

The reason the three categories are singled out for mention is that they have a greater claim to kindness than other categories. Giving them is an obligation upon everyone who has wealth beyond his own sufficiency and the sufficiency of those he supports.

Scholars have differed over whether this verse is muḥkam (not abrogated, Arabic: muḥkam) or mansūkh (abrogated by a later ruling, naskh). It has been said that it is mansūkh, abrogated by the verses of inheritance. It has also been said that it is muḥkam, and that a relative has a binding right in the wealth of a wealthy relative. This is the view of Mujāhid and Qatādah.

Mujāhid said: No charity is accepted from anyone while his kinsman is in need.

Muqātil said: The right of the needy is that he be given charity, and the right of the wayfarer is hospitality.

It has also been said that the "near of kin" in the verse means the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurṭubī said: The first view is more sound, for their right is explained in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:41]. Al-Ḥasan said: The command to give to the near of kin is for recommendation (nadb). ﴿That is best for those who seek the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: that giving is better than withholding for one who seeks closeness to Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning: those who attain what they seek, since they spent for the sake of Allah's Face in obedience to His command.

﴿And what you give in riba﴾. The majority read ātaytum with a long vowel (āytum), meaning "you gave." Mujāhid and Ḥumayd and Ibn Kathīr read it with a short vowel (ataytum), meaning "what you did." They all agree on the long-vowel reading in His saying: ﴿And what you give in zakāh﴾. The root meaning of ribā is increase. The short-vowel reading returns to the meaning of the long-vowel reading, because its meaning is "what you did in the manner of giving," just as you say: "I came in error" and "I came in rightness." The meaning in the verse is: what you give of excess that is free of any return. ﴿So that it may increase within the wealth of people﴾, meaning: so that it may grow and be purified within their wealth. ﴿It does not increase with Allah﴾, meaning: Allah does not bless it.

As-Suddī said: Ribā in this place is the gift that a man gives to his brother seeking a reward in return, for that does not increase with Allah, meaning its giver is not rewarded for it and there is no sin upon him. Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

Al-Wāḥidī said: This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn).

Az-Zajjāj said: That is, a person gives something so that he may be repaid with more than it. That is not forbidden, but there is no reward for it, because the one who gives it seeks in return something greater than it.

Ash-Shaʿbī said: The meaning of the verse is that whatever a person serves another with, in order to benefit from him in his worldly life, that benefit which repays the service does not increase with Allah.

It has been said that this was forbidden to the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not confer favor seeking to receive more﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:6]. Its meaning is: that you give and then take more than it in return.

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the gift given for reward (hibat al-thawāb).

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: And what is similar to it, of what a person does in order to be repaid for it.

ʿIkrimah said: Ribā is of two kinds: a lawful ribā and a forbidden ribā. As for the lawful ribā, it is the gift that a person gives seeking what is better than it, as in this verse.

It has also been said that what is in this verse is the forbidden ribā. According to this view, the meaning of "it does not increase with Allah" is that Allah does not reckon it as increase, but it belongs to the one from whom it was taken.

Al-Muhallab said: The scholars have differed concerning one who gives a gift seeking a reward. Mālik said: It is to be examined. If the one of its kind is one who seeks a reward from the recipient, then he has that right, like the gift of a poor man to a rich man, the gift of a servant to his master, and the gift of a man to his ruler. This is one of the two opinions of ash-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said: He has no reward if he did not stipulate it. This is ash-Shāfiʿī's other opinion.

The majority read liyarbuwa with the letter yā' (third person), with the verb attributed to the pronoun referring to ribā. Nāfiʿ and Yaʿqūb read it with tā' (second person) with a vowel on it, addressing the group, meaning: so that you may become people of increases.

Abū Mālik read: "li-tur'ūhā" [liturbūhā]. The meaning of the verse is that it does not grow with Allah, and He does not reward it, because He accepts only what is intended for His Face sincerely for Him alone. ﴿And what you give in zakāh, seeking the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: (p-1136) and what you give in charity without seeking a return by it, aiming only at what is with Allah. ﴿Those are the ones who multiply﴾. The muḍʿif (one who multiplies) is one who is multiplied beyond the manifold increases of good deeds, those who are given ten times its like up to seven hundredfold.

Al-Farrāʾ said: This is like their saying: muslim (one who has fat camels), mu ʿṭish (one who has thirsty camels), and muḍʿif (one who has weak camels), when he has camels that are fat, or thirsty, or weak.

Ubayy read al-muḍʿafūn with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, as a passive participle (ism mafʿūl).

﴿Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ He, glorified is He, returned to arguing against the polytheists, and that He is the Creator, the Provider, the Causer of death and the Giver of life. Then He said, in the form of a question: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ It is known that they would say: there is none among them who does any of that, so the proof is established against them. Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself transcendent, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate﴾, meaning: they have glorified Him with a true glorification, and He is exalted above being subject to any of that. His saying ﴿of your partners﴾ is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), with min indicating partial (lil-tabʿīḍ). The subject is the relative pronoun: that is, man yaf al (who does). ﴿Of that of yours﴾ is attached to something omitted, because it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the thing mentioned after it. The min in min shayʾ is extra, for emphasis. He attributed the partners to them because they used to call them gods and assign to them a share of their wealth.

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned.﴾ Glorified is He, explained that polytheism and sins are the cause of the appearance of corruption in the world.

Interpreters have differed concerning the meaning of the appearance of the corruption mentioned. It has been said: it is drought, the lack of vegetation, the decrease of provision, the prevalence of fear, and similar things. Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah said: The corruption on land is the killing of the son of Adam his brother, meaning the killing of Qābīl of Hābīl. And at sea it is the king who used to seize every ship by force.

I wonder what proof led them to this distant specification and this strange determination, for the verse was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the definite form of "corruption" indicates the category, so it includes every corruption occurring in the realms of land and sea.

As-Suddī said: The corruption is polytheism, which is the greatest corruption.

It may be said that although polytheism is the complete example among kinds of sins, there is no proof that it is specifically what is meant.

It has also been said: The corruption is the slump of prices and the scarcity of livelihood. It has been said: The corruption is the cutting of roads and oppression. It has been said: other than that, which is specification without proof.

The apparent meaning of the verse is the appearance of whatever it is correct to call corruption, whether it returns to the actions of the children of Adam, their sins, their committing of evil deeds, their severing of ties, their oppression, and their fighting one another, or returns to what comes from Allah, glorified is He, because of their sins, such as drought, prevalence of fear, death, decrease of crops, and decrease of fruits.

Al-barr (land) and al-baḥr (sea) are the well-known things. It has been said: al-barr is the deserts, and al-baḥr is the towns that are on water, as ʿIkrimah said, and the Arabs call great cities "seas." Mujāhid said: al-barr is what is of cities and villages not on a river, and al-baḥr is what is on the bank of a river. The first view is more preferable.

The meaning of al-barr would be the cities of the land, and the meaning of al-baḥr would be the cities of the sea, and what is connected to the cities of their farms and pastures. The bāʾ in ﴿by what﴾ indicates cause, and mā is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). ﴿So that He may make them taste part of what they have done﴾. The lām is connected to ẓahara (appeared), and it is the lām of cause, meaning: so that He may make them taste the punishment of part of their deeds, or the recompense of their deeds. ﴿Perhaps they will return﴾ from what they are engaged in of sins, and repent to Allah.

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before [you].﴾ When Allah, glorified is He, explained the appearance of corruption due to what the hands of the polytheists and the disobedient have earned, He explained to them the misguidance of those like them from people of earlier times, and commanded them to travel so that they might look at their traces and see how their end was. Their dwellings are empty and their lands are desolate and desolate like ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others of the groups of disbelievers. The clause ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾ is a new sentence explaining the condition in which they were, and clarifying the cause by which their end became what it became.

﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes from Allah a Day which cannot be averted.﴾ This is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his community who follow him in it. As if the meaning is: since corruption has appeared by the preceding cause, so set your face, O Muḥammad, etc.

Az-Zajjāj said: Make your direction the following of the upright religion, which is the straight Islam. ﴿Before there comes a Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Which cannot be averted﴾: no one is able to turn it back. Al-maradd is a verbal noun from radda. It has been said: The meaning is: clarify the truth and be thorough in establishing the proofs. ﴿From Allah﴾ is connected to ya'tī (comes), or to something omitted that is indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: no one turns it back from Allah. It has been said: The meaning could be that Allah does not turn it back, because of the connection of His eternal will to its coming, and in this there is weakness and bad manners toward Allah that are not hidden.

﴿On that Day they will be separated.﴾ The original form is yatafaṣṣaʿūn (they will split apart), and at-tafaṣṣuʿ is dispersal. It is said: "the people dispersed" (taṣaddaʿa al-qawm) when they scattered. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And we were like the two boon companions of Jadhīmah for a time of the age, until it was said: they will never separate."

What is meant by their dispersal here is that the people of Paradise will go to Paradise, and the people of the Fire will go to the Fire.

﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾, meaning: the recompense of his disbelief, which is the Fire. ﴿And whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare﴾, meaning: they prepare for themselves places in Paradise by righteous deeds. Al-mihād is the bed, and one says: "I spread the bed, spreading it out" when one lays it out and makes it ready. So He made the righteous deeds, which are the cause of entering Paradise, like building dwellings in Paradise and spreading their bedding.

It has been said: The meaning is: "upon themselves they are compassionate," from the saying about the compassionate one: a mother who spread and then lulled. The placing of the adverbial phrase in both places indicates restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ).

Mujāhid said: ﴿For themselves they prepare﴾ in the grave.

The lām in ﴿that He may reward those who believed﴾ is connected to yatafaṣṣaʿūn, or to yumahhidūn, meaning: they separate so that Allah may reward the believers with what they deserve of His bounty; or they prepare for themselves through righteous deeds so that He may reward them. It has been said: it is connected to something omitted.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Its estimate is "that is so that He may reward," and the reference would be to what preceded in His saying: "whoever does" and "whoever disbelieves."

Abū Ḥayyān made the counterpart (qasīm) of His saying "those who believed and did righteous deeds" an omitted element, indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾, because it is a metonymy for His hatred of them, which requires His anger, glorified is He, and His anger entails His punishment.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verse 38–46 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾. That is: among the indications of the wondrous perfection of His power is the sending of winds as bearers of good news of rain, because they precede it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as a glad tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]. The majority read "al-riyah" (the winds), while al-A'mash read "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular, intending the genus, on account of His saying ﴿bearers of good news﴾. The lam in His saying ﴿and that He may let you taste of His mercy﴾ is connected to "yursil" (He sends), meaning: He sends the winds as bearers of good news, and He sends them that He may let you taste of His mercy, namely the rain and fertility. It was also said that it is connected to a deleted element, meaning: "and that He may let you taste, He sent them." It was also said that the waw is superfluous according to the view of those who permit that, so the lam is connected to "yursil." ﴿And that the ships may run by His command﴾ is coordinated with "li-yudhiqakum min rahmatihi" (that He may let you taste of His mercy), meaning: He sends the winds so that the ships may run upon the sea when they blow. When He attributed the running to the ships, He followed it with His saying "by His command." ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning: that you may seek provision through the trade that the ships carry. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾ for these blessings, so that you single out Allah in worship and increase in obedience.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿And whatever you give in riba﴾ (the verse), that he said: "Riba is of two kinds: riba that is no harm, and riba that is not permissible."
As for the riba that is no harm, it is a man's gift to another man, desiring its excess and multiples.

al-Bayhaqi related from him, who said: "This is the permissible riba: that one gives a gift desiring more than it, and there is neither reward nor sin for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade this specifically, saying: ﴿and do not give, seeking to receive more﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 6]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: ﴿And whatever you give in zakah﴾, he said: "It is the charity."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His saying: ﴿Corruption has appeared on the land and the sea﴾, he said: "The land is the desert that has no river nearby, and the sea is what is of the cities and villages on the bank of a river."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding the verse, he said: "The decrease of blessing due to the deeds of the servants, so that they may repent."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also: ﴿so that they may return﴾, he said: "from sins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: ﴿they will be divided﴾, he said: "they will disperse."

The meaning of the verse is that it does not grow with Allah, and He does not reward it, because He accepts only what is intended for His Face sincerely for Him alone. ﴿And what you give in zakāh, seeking the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: (p-1136) and what you give in charity without seeking a return by it, aiming only at what is with Allah. ﴿Those are the ones who multiply﴾. The muḍʿif (one who multiplies) is one who is multiplied beyond the manifold increases of good deeds, those who are given ten times its like up to seven hundredfold.

Al-Farrāʾ said: This is like their saying: muslim (one who has fat camels), mu ʿṭish (one who has thirsty camels), and muḍʿif (one who has weak camels), when he has camels that are fat, or thirsty, or weak.

Ubayy read al-muḍʿafūn with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, as a passive participle (ism mafʿūl).

﴿Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ He, glorified is He, returned to arguing against the polytheists, and that He is the Creator, the Provider, the Causer of death and the Giver of life. Then He said, in the form of a question: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ It is known that they would say: there is none among them who does any of that, so the proof is established against them. Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself transcendent, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate﴾, meaning: they have glorified Him with a true glorification, and He is exalted above being subject to any of that. His saying ﴿of your partners﴾ is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), with min indicating partial (lil-tabʿīḍ). The subject is the relative pronoun: that is, man yaf al (who does). ﴿Of that of yours﴾ is attached to something omitted, because it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the thing mentioned after it. The min in min shayʾ is extra, for emphasis. He attributed the partners to them because they used to call them gods and assign to them a share of their wealth.

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned.﴾ Glorified is He, explained that polytheism and sins are the cause of the appearance of corruption in the world.

Interpreters have differed concerning the meaning of the appearance of the corruption mentioned. It has been said: it is drought, the lack of vegetation, the decrease of provision, the prevalence of fear, and similar things. Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah said: The corruption on land is the killing of the son of Adam his brother, meaning the killing of Qābīl of Hābīl. And at sea it is the king who used to seize every ship by force.

I wonder what proof led them to this distant specification and this strange determination, for the verse was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the definite form of "corruption" indicates the category, so it includes every corruption occurring in the realms of land and sea.

As-Suddī said: The corruption is polytheism, which is the greatest corruption.

It may be said that although polytheism is the complete example among kinds of sins, there is no proof that it is specifically what is meant.

It has also been said: The corruption is the slump of prices and the scarcity of livelihood. It has been said: The corruption is the cutting of roads and oppression. It has been said: other than that, which is specification without proof.

The apparent meaning of the verse is the appearance of whatever it is correct to call corruption, whether it returns to the actions of the children of Adam, their sins, their committing of evil deeds, their severing of ties, their oppression, and their fighting one another, or returns to what comes from Allah, glorified is He, because of their sins, such as drought, prevalence of fear, death, decrease of crops, and decrease of fruits.

Al-barr (land) and al-baḥr (sea) are the well-known things. It has been said: al-barr is the deserts, and al-baḥr is the towns that are on water, as ʿIkrimah said, and the Arabs call great cities "seas." Mujāhid said: al-barr is what is of cities and villages not on a river, and al-baḥr is what is on the bank of a river. The first view is more preferable.

The meaning of al-barr would be the cities of the land, and the meaning of al-baḥr would be the cities of the sea, and what is connected to the cities of their farms and pastures. The bāʾ in ﴿by what﴾ indicates cause, and mā is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). ﴿So that He may make them taste part of what they have done﴾. The lām is connected to ẓahara (appeared), and it is the lām of cause, meaning: so that He may make them taste the punishment of part of their deeds, or the recompense of their deeds. ﴿Perhaps they will return﴾ from what they are engaged in of sins, and repent to Allah.

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before [you].﴾ When Allah, glorified is He, explained the appearance of corruption due to what the hands of the polytheists and the disobedient have earned, He explained to them the misguidance of those like them from people of earlier times, and commanded them to travel so that they might look at their traces and see how their end was. Their dwellings are empty and their lands are desolate and desolate like ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others of the groups of disbelievers. The clause ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾ is a new sentence explaining the condition in which they were, and clarifying the cause by which their end became what it became.

It has been said: The meaning is: clarify the truth and be thorough in establishing the proofs. ﴿From Allah﴾ is connected to ya'tī (comes), or to something omitted that is indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: no one turns it back from Allah. It has been said: The meaning could be that Allah does not turn it back, because of the connection of His eternal will to its coming, and in this there is weakness and bad manners toward Allah that are not hidden.

What is meant by their dispersal here is that the people of Paradise will go to Paradise, and the people of the Fire will go to the Fire.

So He made the righteous deeds, which are the cause of entering Paradise, like building dwellings in Paradise and spreading their bedding.

Mujāhid said: ﴿For themselves they prepare﴾ in the grave.

It has been said: it is connected to something omitted.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Its estimate is "that is so that He may reward," and the reference would be to what preceded in His saying: "whoever does" and "whoever disbelieves."

When He attributed the running to the ships, He followed it with His saying "by His command." ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning: that you may seek provision through the trade that the ships carry. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾ for these blessings, so that you single out Allah in worship and increase in obedience.

As for the riba that is no harm, it is a man's gift to another man, desiring its excess and multiples.

al-Bayhaqi related from him, who said: "This is the permissible riba: that one gives a gift desiring more than it, and there is neither reward nor sin for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade this specifically, saying: ﴿and do not give, seeking to receive more﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 6]."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: ﴿And whatever you give in zakah﴾, he said: "It is the charity."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding His saying: ﴿Corruption has appeared on the land and the sea﴾, he said: "The land is the desert that has no river nearby, and the sea is what is of the cities and villages on the bank of a river."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding the verse, he said: "The decrease of blessing due to the deeds of the servants, so that they may repent."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also: ﴿so that they may return﴾, he said: "from sins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: ﴿they will be divided﴾, he said: "they will disperse."

When Allah, glorified is He, explained how the command of Allah should be honored, He pointed to what is due in support of kin and those in need, from among those whom Allah has granted abundance in provision. So He said: ﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community, who follow him in this, or to every responsible person who has wealth that Allah has made abundant for him. He gave precedence to kindness toward relatives, because the best charity is that given to a near relative. It is a charity that is multiplied, and it is also the maintaining of ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim), which is recommended. What is meant is kindness toward them through charity, maintaining ties, and righteousness. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾, meaning: give the needy and the wayfarer their right, which they deserve.

The reason the three categories are singled out for mention is that they have a greater claim to kindness than other categories. Giving them is an obligation upon everyone who has wealth beyond his own sufficiency and the sufficiency of those he supports.

Scholars have differed over whether this verse is muḥkam (not abrogated, Arabic: muḥkam) or mansūkh (abrogated by a later ruling, naskh). It has been said that it is mansūkh, abrogated by the verses of inheritance. It has also been said that it is muḥkam, and that a relative has a binding right in the wealth of a wealthy relative. This is the view of Mujāhid and Qatādah.

Mujāhid said: No charity is accepted from anyone while his kinsman is in need.

Muqātil said: The right of the needy is that he be given charity, and the right of the wayfarer is hospitality.

It has also been said that the "near of kin" in the verse means the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurṭubī said: The first view is more sound, for their right is explained in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:41]. Al-Ḥasan said: The command to give to the near of kin is for recommendation (nadb). ﴿That is best for those who seek the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: that giving is better than withholding for one who seeks closeness to Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning: those who attain what they seek, since they spent for the sake of Allah's Face in obedience to His command.

﴿And what you give in riba﴾. The majority read ātaytum with a long vowel (āytum), meaning "you gave." Mujāhid and Ḥumayd and Ibn Kathīr read it with a short vowel (ataytum), meaning "what you did." They all agree on the long-vowel reading in His saying: ﴿And what you give in zakāh﴾. The root meaning of ribā is increase. The short-vowel reading returns to the meaning of the long-vowel reading, because its meaning is "what you did in the manner of giving," just as you say: "I came in error" and "I came in rightness." The meaning in the verse is: what you give of excess that is free of any return. ﴿So that it may increase within the wealth of people﴾, meaning: so that it may grow and be purified within their wealth. ﴿It does not increase with Allah﴾, meaning: Allah does not bless it.

As-Suddī said: Ribā in this place is the gift that a man gives to his brother seeking a reward in return, for that does not increase with Allah, meaning its giver is not rewarded for it and there is no sin upon him. Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

Al-Wāḥidī said: This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn).

Az-Zajjāj said: That is, a person gives something so that he may be repaid with more than it. That is not forbidden, but there is no reward for it, because the one who gives it seeks in return something greater than it.

Ash-Shaʿbī said: The meaning of the verse is that whatever a person serves another with, in order to benefit from him in his worldly life, that benefit which repays the service does not increase with Allah.

It has been said that this was forbidden to the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not confer favor seeking to receive more﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:6]. Its meaning is: that you give and then take more than it in return.

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the gift given for reward (hibat al-thawāb).

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: And what is similar to it, of what a person does in order to be repaid for it.

ʿIkrimah said: Ribā is of two kinds: a lawful ribā and a forbidden ribā. As for the lawful ribā, it is the gift that a person gives seeking what is better than it, as in this verse.

It has also been said that what is in this verse is the forbidden ribā. According to this view, the meaning of "it does not increase with Allah" is that Allah does not reckon it as increase, but it belongs to the one from whom it was taken.

Al-Muhallab said: The scholars have differed concerning one who gives a gift seeking a reward. Mālik said: It is to be examined. If the one of its kind is one who seeks a reward from the recipient, then he has that right, like the gift of a poor man to a rich man, the gift of a servant to his master, and the gift of a man to his ruler. This is one of the two opinions of ash-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said: He has no reward if he did not stipulate it. This is ash-Shāfiʿī's other opinion.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also: ﴿so that they may return﴾, he said: "from sins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: ﴿they will be divided﴾, he said: "they will disperse."

When Allah, glorified is He, explained how the command of Allah should be honored, He pointed to what is due in support of kin and those in need, from among those whom Allah has granted abundance in provision. So He said: ﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community, who follow him in this, or to every responsible person who has wealth that Allah has made abundant for him. He gave precedence to kindness toward relatives, because the best charity is that given to a near relative. It is a charity that is multiplied, and it is also the maintaining of ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim), which is recommended. What is meant is kindness toward them through charity, maintaining ties, and righteousness. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾, meaning: give the needy and the wayfarer their right, which they deserve.

The reason the three categories are singled out for mention is that they have a greater claim to kindness than other categories. Giving them is an obligation upon everyone who has wealth beyond his own sufficiency and the sufficiency of those he supports.

Scholars have differed over whether this verse is muḥkam (not abrogated, Arabic: muḥkam) or mansūkh (abrogated by a later ruling, naskh). It has been said that it is mansūkh, abrogated by the verses of inheritance. It has also been said that it is muḥkam, and that a relative has a binding right in the wealth of a wealthy relative. This is the view of Mujāhid and Qatādah.

Mujāhid said: No charity is accepted from anyone while his kinsman is in need.

Muqātil said: The right of the needy is that he be given charity, and the right of the wayfarer is hospitality.

It has also been said that the "near of kin" in the verse means the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurṭubī said: The first view is more sound, for their right is explained in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:41]. Al-Ḥasan said: The command to give to the near of kin is for recommendation (nadb). ﴿That is best for those who seek the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: that giving is better than withholding for one who seeks closeness to Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning: those who attain what they seek, since they spent for the sake of Allah's Face in obedience to His command.

﴿And what you give in riba﴾. The majority read ātaytum with a long vowel (āytum), meaning "you gave." Mujāhid and Ḥumayd and Ibn Kathīr read it with a short vowel (ataytum), meaning "what you did." They all agree on the long-vowel reading in His saying: ﴿And what you give in zakāh﴾. The root meaning of ribā is increase. The short-vowel reading returns to the meaning of the long-vowel reading, because its meaning is "what you did in the manner of giving," just as you say: "I came in error" and "I came in rightness." The meaning in the verse is: what you give of excess that is free of any return. ﴿So that it may increase within the wealth of people﴾, meaning: so that it may grow and be purified within their wealth. ﴿It does not increase with Allah﴾, meaning: Allah does not bless it.

As-Suddī said: Ribā in this place is the gift that a man gives to his brother seeking a reward in return, for that does not increase with Allah, meaning its giver is not rewarded for it and there is no sin upon him. Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

Al-Wāḥidī said: This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirūn).

Az-Zajjāj said: That is, a person gives something so that he may be repaid with more than it. That is not forbidden, but there is no reward for it, because the one who gives it seeks in return something greater than it.

Ash-Shaʿbī said: The meaning of the verse is that whatever a person serves another with, in order to benefit from him in his worldly life, that benefit which repays the service does not increase with Allah.

It has been said that this was forbidden to the Prophet (ﷺ) specifically, based on His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not confer favor seeking to receive more﴾ [al-Muddaththir 74:6]. Its meaning is: that you give and then take more than it in return.

It has been said that this verse was revealed concerning the gift given for reward (hibat al-thawāb).

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: And what is similar to it, of what a person does in order to be repaid for it.

ʿIkrimah said: Ribā is of two kinds: a lawful ribā and a forbidden ribā. As for the lawful ribā, it is the gift that a person gives seeking what is better than it, as in this verse.

It has also been said that what is in this verse is the forbidden ribā. According to this view, the meaning of "it does not increase with Allah" is that Allah does not reckon it as increase, but it belongs to the one from whom it was taken.

Al-Muhallab said: The scholars have differed concerning one who gives a gift seeking a reward. Mālik said: It is to be examined. If the one of its kind is one who seeks a reward from the recipient, then he has that right, like the gift of a poor man to a rich man, the gift of a servant to his master, and the gift of a man to his ruler. This is one of the two opinions of ash-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah said: He has no reward if he did not stipulate it. This is ash-Shāfiʿī's other opinion.

The majority read liyarbuwa with the letter yā' (third person), with the verb attributed to the pronoun referring to ribā. Nāfiʿ and Yaʿqūb read it with tā' (second person) with a vowel on it, addressing the group, meaning: so that you may become people of increases.

Abū Mālik read: "li-tur'ūhā" [liturbūhā]. The meaning of the verse is that it does not grow with Allah, and He does not reward it, because He accepts only what is intended for His Face sincerely for Him alone. ﴿And what you give in zakāh, seeking the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: (p-1136) and what you give in charity without seeking a return by it, aiming only at what is with Allah. ﴿Those are the ones who multiply﴾. The muḍʿif (one who multiplies) is one who is multiplied beyond the manifold increases of good deeds, those who are given ten times its like up to seven hundredfold.

Al-Farrāʾ said: This is like their saying: muslim (one who has fat camels), mu ʿṭish (one who has thirsty camels), and muḍʿif (one who has weak camels), when he has camels that are fat, or thirsty, or weak.

Ubayy read al-muḍʿafūn with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, as a passive participle (ism mafʿūl).

﴿Allah is the One who created you, then provided for you, then causes you to die, then gives you life. Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ He, glorified is He, returned to arguing against the polytheists, and that He is the Creator, the Provider, the Causer of death and the Giver of life. Then He said, in the form of a question: ﴿Is there any of your partners who does any of that?﴾ It is known that they would say: there is none among them who does any of that, so the proof is established against them. Then He, glorified is He, declared Himself transcendent, saying: ﴿Glory be to Him and exalted above what they associate﴾, meaning: they have glorified Him with a true glorification, and He is exalted above being subject to any of that. His saying ﴿of your partners﴾ is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam), with min indicating partial (lil-tabʿīḍ). The subject is the relative pronoun: that is, man yaf al (who does). ﴿Of that of yours﴾ is attached to something omitted, because it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the thing mentioned after it. The min in min shayʾ is extra, for emphasis. He attributed the partners to them because they used to call them gods and assign to them a share of their wealth.

﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea by what the hands of people have earned.﴾ Glorified is He, explained that polytheism and sins are the cause of the appearance of corruption in the world.

Interpreters have differed concerning the meaning of the appearance of the corruption mentioned. It has been said: it is drought, the lack of vegetation, the decrease of provision, the prevalence of fear, and similar things. Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah said: The corruption on land is the killing of the son of Adam his brother, meaning the killing of Qābīl of Hābīl. And at sea it is the king who used to seize every ship by force.

I wonder what proof led them to this distant specification and this strange determination, for the verse was revealed to Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the definite form of "corruption" indicates the category, so it includes every corruption occurring in the realms of land and sea.

As-Suddī said: The corruption is polytheism, which is the greatest corruption.

It may be said that although polytheism is the complete example among kinds of sins, there is no proof that it is specifically what is meant.

It has also been said: The corruption is the slump of prices and the scarcity of livelihood. It has been said: The corruption is the cutting of roads and oppression. It has been said: other than that, which is specification without proof.

The apparent meaning of the verse is the appearance of whatever it is correct to call corruption, whether it returns to the actions of the children of Adam, their sins, their committing of evil deeds, their severing of ties, their oppression, and their fighting one another, or returns to what comes from Allah, glorified is He, because of their sins, such as drought, prevalence of fear, death, decrease of crops, and decrease of fruits.

Al-barr (land) and al-baḥr (sea) are the well-known things. It has been said: al-barr is the deserts, and al-baḥr is the towns that are on water, as ʿIkrimah said, and the Arabs call great cities "seas." Mujāhid said: al-barr is what is of cities and villages not on a river, and al-baḥr is what is on the bank of a river. The first view is more preferable.

The meaning of al-barr would be the cities of the land, and the meaning of al-baḥr would be the cities of the sea, and what is connected to the cities of their farms and pastures. The bāʾ in ﴿by what﴾ indicates cause, and mā is either a relative pronoun or a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). ﴿So that He may make them taste part of what they have done﴾. The lām is connected to ẓahara (appeared), and it is the lām of cause, meaning: so that He may make them taste the punishment of part of their deeds, or the recompense of their deeds. ﴿Perhaps they will return﴾ from what they are engaged in of sins, and repent to Allah.

﴿Say: Travel through the earth and observe how was the end of those before [you].﴾ When Allah, glorified is He, explained the appearance of corruption due to what the hands of the polytheists and the disobedient have earned, He explained to them the misguidance of those like them from people of earlier times, and commanded them to travel so that they might look at their traces and see how their end was. Their dwellings are empty and their lands are desolate and desolate like ʿĀd, Thamūd, and others of the groups of disbelievers. The clause ﴿most of them were polytheists﴾ is a new sentence explaining the condition in which they were, and clarifying the cause by which their end became what it became.

﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes from Allah a Day which cannot be averted.﴾ This is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his community who follow him in it. As if the meaning is: since corruption has appeared by the preceding cause, so set your face, O Muḥammad, etc.

Az-Zajjāj said: Make your direction the following of the upright religion, which is the straight Islam. ﴿Before there comes a Day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Which cannot be averted﴾: no one is able to turn it back. Al-maradd is a verbal noun from radda. It has been said: The meaning is: clarify the truth and be thorough in establishing the proofs. ﴿From Allah﴾ is connected to ya'tī (comes), or to something omitted that is indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: no one turns it back from Allah. It has been said: The meaning could be that Allah does not turn it back, because of the connection of His eternal will to its coming, and in this there is weakness and bad manners toward Allah that are not hidden.

﴿On that Day they will be separated.﴾ The original form is yatafaṣṣaʿūn (they will split apart), and at-tafaṣṣuʿ is dispersal. It is said: "the people dispersed" (taṣaddaʿa al-qawm) when they scattered. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And we were like the two boon companions of Jadhīmah for a time of the age, until it was said: they will never separate."

What is meant by their dispersal here is that the people of Paradise will go to Paradise, and the people of the Fire will go to the Fire.

﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾, meaning: the recompense of his disbelief, which is the Fire. ﴿And whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare﴾, meaning: they prepare for themselves places in Paradise by righteous deeds. Al-mihād is the bed, and one says: "I spread the bed, spreading it out" when one lays it out and makes it ready. So He made the righteous deeds, which are the cause of entering Paradise, like building dwellings in Paradise and spreading their bedding.

It has been said: The meaning is: "upon themselves they are compassionate," from the saying about the compassionate one: a mother who spread and then lulled. The placing of the adverbial phrase in both places indicates restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ).

Mujāhid said: ﴿For themselves they prepare﴾ in the grave.

The lām in ﴿that He may reward those who believed﴾ is connected to yatafaṣṣaʿūn, or to yumahhidūn, meaning: they separate so that Allah may reward the believers with what they deserve of His bounty; or they prepare for themselves through righteous deeds so that He may reward them. It has been said: it is connected to something omitted.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Its estimate is "that is so that He may reward," and the reference would be to what preceded in His saying: "whoever does" and "whoever disbelieves."

Abū Ḥayyān made the counterpart (qasīm) of His saying "those who believed and did righteous deeds" an omitted element, indicated by His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾, because it is a metonymy for His hatred of them, which requires His anger, glorified is He, and His anger entails His punishment.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 30, verse 38–46 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾. That is: among the indications of the wondrous perfection of His power is the sending of winds as bearers of good news of rain, because they precede it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as a glad tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57]. The majority read "al-riyah" (the winds), while al-A'mash read "al-rih" (the wind) in the singular, intending the genus, on account of His saying ﴿bearers of good news﴾. The lam in His saying ﴿and that He may let you taste of His mercy﴾ is connected to "yursil" (He sends), meaning: He sends the winds as bearers of good news, and He sends them that He may let you taste of His mercy, namely the rain and fertility. It was also said that it is connected to a deleted element, meaning: "and that He may let you taste, He sent them." It was also said that the waw is superfluous according to the view of those who permit that, so the lam is connected to "yursil." ﴿And that the ships may run by His command﴾ is coordinated with "li-yudhiqakum min rahmatihi" (that He may let you taste of His mercy), meaning: He sends the winds so that the ships may run upon the sea when they blow. When He attributed the running to the ships, He followed it with His saying "by His command." ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾, meaning: that you may seek provision through the trade that the ships carry. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾ for these blessings, so that you single out Allah in worship and increase in obedience.

It has been said: The meaning is: clarify the truth and be thorough in establishing the proofs. ﴿From Allah﴾ is connected to ya'tī (comes), or to something omitted that is indicated by the verbal noun, meaning: no one turns it back from Allah. "And we were like the two boon companions of Jadhīmah for a time of the age, until it was said: they will never separate."

What is meant by their dispersal here is that the people of Paradise will go to Paradise, and the people of the Fire will go to the Fire.

﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾, meaning: the recompense of his disbelief, which is the Fire. ﴿And whoever does righteousness, for themselves they prepare﴾, meaning: they prepare for themselves places in Paradise by righteous deeds. Al-mihād is the bed, and one says: "I spread the bed, spreading it out" when one lays it out and makes it ready. So He made the righteous deeds, which are the cause of entering Paradise, like building dwellings in Paradise and spreading their bedding.

It has been said: The meaning is: "upon themselves they are compassionate," from the saying about the compassionate one: a mother who spread and then lulled. The placing of the adverbial phrase in both places indicates restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ).

Mujāhid said: ﴿For themselves they prepare﴾ in the grave.

The lām in ﴿that He may reward those who believed﴾ is connected to yatafaṣṣaʿūn, or to yumahhidūn, meaning: they separate so that Allah may reward the believers with what they deserve of His bounty; or they prepare for themselves through righteous deeds so that He may reward them. It has been said: it is connected to something omitted.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: Its estimate is "that is so that He may reward," and the reference would be to what preceded in His saying: "whoever does" and "whoever disbelieves."

﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also regarding the verse, he said: "The decrease of blessing due to the deeds of the servants, so that they may repent."

Ibn al-Mundhir related from him also: ﴿so that they may return﴾, he said: "from sins."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him also: ﴿they will be divided﴾, he said: "they will disperse."

When Allah, glorified is He, explained how the command of Allah should be honored, He pointed to what is due in support of kin and those in need, from among those whom Allah has granted abundance in provision. So He said: ﴿So give the near of kin his right﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community, who follow him in this, or to every responsible person who has wealth that Allah has made abundant for him. He gave precedence to kindness toward relatives, because the best charity is that given to a near relative. It is a charity that is multiplied, and it is also the maintaining of ties of kinship (ṣilat al-raḥim), which is recommended. What is meant is kindness toward them through charity, maintaining ties, and righteousness. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾, meaning: give the needy and the wayfarer their right, which they deserve.

The reason the three categories are singled out for mention is that they have a greater claim to kindness than other categories. Giving them is an obligation upon everyone who has wealth beyond his own sufficiency and the sufficiency of those he supports.

Scholars have differed over whether this verse is muḥkam (not abrogated, Arabic: muḥkam) or mansūkh (abrogated by a later ruling, naskh). It has been said that it is mansūkh, abrogated by the verses of inheritance. It has also been said that it is muḥkam, and that a relative has a binding right in the wealth of a wealthy relative. This is the view of Mujāhid and Qatādah.

Mujāhid said: No charity is accepted from anyone while his kinsman is in need.

Muqātil said: The right of the needy is that he be given charity, and the right of the wayfarer is hospitality.

It has also been said that the "near of kin" in the verse means the Prophet (ﷺ).

Al-Qurṭubī said: The first view is more sound, for their right is explained in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in His saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:41]. Al-Ḥasan said: The command to give to the near of kin is for recommendation (nadb). ﴿That is best for those who seek the Face of Allah﴾, meaning: that giving is better than withholding for one who seeks closeness to Allah, glorified is He. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, meaning: those who attain what they seek, since they spent for the sake of Allah's Face in obedience to His command.
